problems.title: Potential energy curves and molecular orbitals
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (13 marks). Potential energy curves and molecular orbitals

J. G. Dojahn, E. M. C. Chen and W.E. Wenthworth [J. Phys. Chem. 100, 9649 (1996)] examined the potential energy diagrams of $\ce{X2}$ and $\ce{X2^-}$ where X is a halogen. The diagram for $\ce{F2}$ and $\ce{F2^-}$ is reproduced on the next page.

1.1 (1 mark) From this diagram, the dissociation energies (in eV) of $\ce{F2}$ and $\ce{F2^-}$ are (Mark X in the correct box)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{F2} & 1.2 & 1.3 & 1.6 & 1.8 & 1.9 \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{F2^-} & 1.1 & 1.3 & 1.5 & 1.6 & 1.7 \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{F2}\ \text{molecule} & 2.8 & 3.0 & 3.2 & 3.3 & 3.4 \end{array}$$

1.4 (2 marks) The vibrational frequencies for $\ce{F2}$ and $\ce{F2^-}$ reported by Dojahn et al. on fitting the potential energy curves were 917 and $450\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. What is the ratio of the corresponding force constants?

1.6 (1 mark) The bond orders in $\ce{F2}$ and $\ce{F2^-}$ are respectively

• $\ce{N2}$

problems.title: Unsaturated compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (19 marks). Unsaturated compounds

Alkenes and alkynes are collectively referred to as unsaturated compounds, as they contain less hydrogen atoms compared to the corresponding alkanes. Alkenes are also called olefins, a term derived from olefiant gas, meaning oil forming gas. This term originated due to the oily appearance of alkene derivatives. Compared to alkenes, alkynes are not so common in nature, but some plants use alkynes to protect themselves against diseases or predators.

2.1 (2 marks) Give the IUPAC names with stereochemical descriptors (E/Z) for each of the following compounds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-2-fig1.png

2.2 (1 mark) The following compound $\mathbf{A}$ can be prepared by the addition of $\ce{HBr}$ to either of two alkenes $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. Give the structures of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-2-fig2.png

2.3 (2 marks) Draw the energy profile diagram of the reaction of $\ce{HBr}$ with either $\mathbf{B}$ or $\mathbf{C}$ in question 2.2. Label the intermediate/s and transition state/s.

2.4 (1.5 marks) Indicate the relationship between the compounds in each of the following pairs, as homomers ($\mathbf{H}$), enantiomers ($\mathbf{E}$) or diastereomers ($\mathbf{D}$). Write the corresponding alphabet in the box.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-2-fig3.png

2.5 (2.5 marks) Heats of hydrogenation indicates the relative stability of alkenes. Match the list of compounds given in column A with the corresponding heats of hydrogenation listed in column B

$$\begin{array}{ll} \textbf{Column A} & \textbf{Column B}\ (\mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}}) \\ \text{a) } \ce{CH2=CHCH2CH=CH2} & \text{i) } -226 \\ \text{b) } \ce{CH3-CH=C=CHCH3} & \text{ii) } -119 \\ \text{c) } \ce{CH2=C(CH3)-CH2CH3} & \text{iii) } -295 \\ \text{d) } \ce{CH3-C(CH3)=CHCH3} & \text{iv) } -252 \\ \text{e) } \ce{CH2=CH-CH=CHCH3} & \text{v) } -113 \end{array}$$

2.6 (1 mark) Draw the structure of the product/s formed when the following compound is subjected to ozonolysis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-2-fig4.png

2.7 (3 marks) An optically active alkyne $\mathbf{D}$ has 89.52% carbon. Compound $\mathbf{D}$ can be catalytically hydrogenated to n-butylcyclohexane. Treatment of $\mathbf{D}$ with $\ce{C2H5MgBr}$ liberates no gas. Catalytic hydrogenation of $\mathbf{D}$ over Pd/C in the presence of quinoline (a catalyst poison) and treatment of the product with ozone and then $\ce{H2O2}$ gives an optically active tricarboxylic acid $\mathbf{E}$ ($\ce{C8H12O6}$). Compound $\mathbf{E}$ on heating undergoes dehydration by loss of a molecule of water to give $\mathbf{F}$. Draw the possible structures of $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$.

2.8 (4 marks) When equimolar amounts of 1,3-butadiene and bromine are reacted at high temperature, two compounds $\mathbf{G}$ (major) and $\mathbf{H}$ (minor) with the formula $\ce{C4H6Br2}$ are formed. Compound $\mathbf{G}$ reacts with more $\ce{Br2}$ to form compound $\mathbf{I}$ ($\ce{C4H6Br4}$) which proved to be a meso compound. Compound $\mathbf{H}$ reacts with more $\ce{Br2}$ to form both $\mathbf{I}$ and a diastereomer $\mathbf{J}$. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. Draw the Fischer projection for $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ indicating the stereochemistry (with R/S designation) of the chiral carbons.

2.9 (1 mark) Diels-Alder reaction of 2,5-dimethylfuran and maleic anhydride gives compound $\mathbf{K}$ which can exist in two stereoisomeric forms. Draw the structures of the two isomers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-2-fig5.png

2.10 (1 mark) Compound $\mathbf{K}$ undergoes acid catalysed dehydration to give $\mathbf{L}$ ($\ce{C10H8O3}$). Draw the structure of $\mathbf{L}$.

In 1825, Michael Faraday isolated benzene for the first time from the oily mixture that condensed from illuminating gas (the fuel burnt in gas lights). Subsequently many compounds related to benzene were discovered. These compounds had typical odours (aroma) and hence this group of compounds was called aromatic.

Similar compounds possessing $(4n)\pi$ electrons are highly unstable and are called antiaromatic compounds. It is interesting that compounds adjust their 3D and electronic structures to lower their energies. Answer the following by marking X in the correct box.

problems.title: Reaction stoichiometry, kinetics and thermodynamics
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (15 marks). Reaction stoichiometry, kinetics and thermodynamics

Nitrosyl chloride ($\ce{NOCl}$), is a yellow gas that is most commonly encountered as a decomposition product of aqua regia. It is toxic and irritating to the lungs. On heating $\ce{NOCl}$ decomposes as $\ce{2NOCl -> 2NO + Cl2}$.

The enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) for the formation of 1 mole of $\ce{Cl2}$ by the decomposition of $\ce{NOCl}$ is 75.3 kJ between 100 K to 600 K. The standard entropies ($S^0_{298\,\mathrm{K}}$) of different species are as given below:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} \text{Substance} & \ce{NOCl} & \ce{NO} & \ce{Cl2} \\ \hline S^0_{298}\ \mathrm{J/K} & 264 & 211 & 223 \end{array}$$

4.1 (2 marks) Calculate $K_\mathrm{p}$ of the above decomposition reaction at 298 K.

4.2 (1 mark) Calculate the temperature at which $K_\mathrm{p}$ will be double the value at 298 K.

4.3 (1 mark) Calculate the temperature above which the reaction will become spontaneous.

4.4 (2.5 marks) A gaseous mixture of $\ce{NO}$, $\ce{Cl2}$ and $\ce{NOCl}$ with partial pressures (in bar) 1.5, 0.88 and 0.065 respectively was taken at 475 K. Deduce whether the net reaction will lead to increase in $\ce{NOCl}$ concentration.

4.5 (1 mark) The initial rates of the reaction $\ce{2NO + Cl2 -> 2NOCl}$ at different initial concentrations of the reactants are given below.

$$\begin{array}{lll} [\ce{NO(g)}]\ (\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) & [\ce{Cl2(g)}]\ (\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) & \text{Initial Rate}\ (\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}) \\ 0.250 & 0.250 & 1.43\times10^{-6} \\ 0.250 & 0.500 & 2.86\times10^{-6} \\ 0.500 & 0.500 & 11.4\times10^{-6} \end{array}$$

Write the kinetic rate law.

4.6 (1.5 marks) The rate constant for the formation of $\ce{NOCl}$ at 400 K is $2.0\times10^{4}$ times the value at 300 K. Calculate the activation energy for the reaction.

4.7 (3 marks) The following mechanisms (I and II) were proposed for the formation of $\ce{NOCl}$.

Mechanism I

$$\ce{NO + NO} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{N2O2}\ \text{(fast equilibrium)}$$

$$\ce{N2O2 + Cl2} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{2NOCl}\ \text{(slow)}$$

Mechanism II

$$\ce{NO + Cl2} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{NOCl2}\ \text{(fast equilibrium)}$$

$$\ce{NO + NOCl2} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{2NOCl}\ \text{(slow)}$$

Deduce which mechanism/s is/are consistent with the rate law arrived at in 4.5.

4.8 (1.5 marks) The extent of a reaction is defined as $(n_i - n_i^0)/\nu_i$ where $n_i^0$ and $n_i$ are the number of moles of reactant or product (species i) present respectively at the commencement of the reaction ($t = 0$) and at any time, $t$. $\nu_i$ is the stoichiometric coefficient of the substance "i" in the balanced equation. For the calculation of the extent of reaction, the stoichiometric coefficient is considered to be positive for products and negative for reactants. The extent of the reaction is the same for all reactants and products.

For the reaction, $\ce{2NO + Cl2 -> 2NOCl}$, when 0.39 mol, 0.28 mol and 0.13 mol of $\ce{NO}$, $\ce{Cl2}$ and $\ce{NOCl}$ respectively were taken initially, after certain time 0.18 mol of $\ce{Cl2}$ was found to remain in the reaction mixture. Calculate the extent of reaction with respect to $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NOCl}$.

4.9 (1.5 marks) When reactants are not taken in stoichiometric proportions, a reaction will go to completion when one of the reactants is completely consumed. This reagent is known as the limiting reagent which will have the lowest value for $n_i^0/|\nu_i|$. What is the limiting reagent in (4.8)? Calculate the extent of the reaction in (4.8), with respect to $\ce{NOCl}$, when the reaction goes to completion.

problems.title: Phase equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (14 marks). Phase equilibrium

Phase diagram of a one-component system ($\mathbf{S}$), is shown below. Answer the following questions with the help of this diagram.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2008-5-fig1.png

5.1 (1 mark) What kind of phase change will take place if solid $\mathbf{S}$ is kept in the open under normal condition? (Mark X in the correct box)

a) Sublimation

b) Melting

c) Evaporation

d) No change

5.2 (1 mark) Under which condition, are all the three phases of the system $\mathbf{S}$ in equilibrium? (Mark X in the correct box).

a) $T > 304.2\,\mathrm{K}$ and $P > 72.9$ atmosphere

b) $T = 216.8\,\mathrm{K}$ and $P = 5.2$ atmosphere

c) $T > 304.2\,\mathrm{K}$

d) $P > 72.9$ atmosphere

5.3 (2 marks) Temperature of the system at $\mathrm{X_1}$ is increased at constant pressure to reach $\mathrm{X_4}$. What are the phase/s of the system at the four different states $\mathrm{X_1}$ to $\mathrm{X_4}$?

5.4 (2 marks) Show graphically the heating curve (Temperature vs. Time) for the process in the above problem (5.3) with appropriate labeling of physical states.

5.5 (1 mark) If pressure is increased, the melting temperature of solid $\mathbf{S}$ will (Mark X in the correct box)

a) Not change

b) Increase

c) Decrease

5.6 (1 mark) With the help of Clapeyron equation for phase change ($\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T = \Delta H^\circ/T\Delta V$), find what happens to the volume of the system at $\mathrm{X_2}$ on heating?

5.7 (1 mark) What is the state of the system $\mathbf{S}$, if it is heated in a sealed container above the critical temperature (304.2 K)?

5.8 (1 mark) What happens to the system $\mathbf{S}$ at $\mathrm{X_5}$, if pressure is changed slowly keeping temperature constant? (Mark X in the correct box)

a) At a higher pressure, the system will become liquid.

b) At a lower pressure, the system will become liquid.

c) The system will be in the same phase.

Solutions

5.9 (1 mark) Raoult's law states that the partial pressure ($p_1$) of a solvent over a solution is given by the vapor pressure ($p_1^0$) of the pure solvent times the mole fraction ($\chi_1$) of the solvent. Derive an expression relating lowering of vapor pressure with solute mole fraction.

5.10 (1 mark) The vapor pressure of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is 17.54 mm of Hg and that of 10% (w/w) solution of an organic solute at the same temperature is 16.93 mm of Hg. Calculate the molecular weight of the solute using the expression derived in 5.9.

5.11 A solute is dissolved in two immiscible liquids in contact. Nernst's distribution law states that at equilibrium, the ratio of the concentration of the same molecular species in the two phases is constant ($K_\mathrm{D}$) at constant temperature.

Solute $\mathbf{A}$ is present as monomeric species $\mathbf{A}$ in solvent $\mathbf{S_1}$ and associates to form $\mathbf{A_n}$ in solvent $\mathbf{S_2}$. Species A and $\mathrm{A_n}$ are in equilibrium with an equilibrium constant $K$.

a) (1 mark) What is the concentration of $\mathbf{A}$ in solvent $\mathbf{S_2}$, if concentration of $\mathbf{A_n}$ is $\mathbf{C_2}$?

b) (1 mark) If the concentration of $\mathbf{A}$ in solvent $\mathbf{S_1}$ is $\mathbf{C_1}$, calculate the distribution constant $K_\mathrm{D}$ of the solute.

problems.title: Chemistry of Phosphorus and its compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (13 marks). Chemistry of Phosphorus and its compounds

Elemental phosphorus is recovered from the minerals flurapatite and hydroxyapatite by carbon arc reduction. The resulting white phosphorus is a solid consisting of $\ce{P4}$ molecules.

6.1 (1 mark) Draw the geometrical and Lewis structures of $\ce{P4}$.

6.2 (1 mark) White phosphorus reacts vigorously with aqueous sodium hydroxide resulting in the evolution of a gas and formation of sodium hypophosphite. Write the balanced equation for this reaction.

6.3 (3 marks) Sodium hypophosphite and sodium phosphite contain oxoanions of phosphorus.

a) Draw structures of these oxoanions.

b) State whether these oxoanions will act as an oxidizing agent or a reducing agent. (Mark X in the correct box)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \text{Oxidising agent} & \text{Reducing agent} \\ \hline \text{hypophosphite} & & \\ \hline \text{phosphite} & & \end{array}$$

c) Give appropriate reasons for your answers.

6.4 (0.5 mark) $\ce{H3PO4}$ can be synthesized by the reaction of hydroxyapatite ($\ce{Ca5(PO4)3F}$) with $\ce{H2SO4}$. Write balanced equation for this reaction.

Complete combustion of phosphorus yields phosphorus(V) oxide $\ce{P4O10}$, that has a cage structure.

6.5 (2 marks) Draw the structure of $\ce{P4O10}$.

6.6 (1 mark) Calcium oxide reacts with $\ce{P4O10}$ to form calcium phosphate. Calculate the amount of $\ce{CaO}$ required (in grams) to react with 426 g of $\ce{P4O10}$.

Halides of phosphorus play an important role in the synthesis of a variety of phosphorus compounds.

6.7 (1 mark) Write balanced equation/s for the formation of triethyl phosphate from phosphorus trichloride.

6.8 (2.5 marks) Show the electronic configurations of P atom in i) ground and ii) excited states. State the hybridization of orbitals of P atom in $\ce{PCl3}$ and $\ce{PCl5}$ molecules. Predict the geometry of $\ce{PCl5}$.

6.9 (1 mark) $\ce{PCl5}$ can react with $\ce{NH4Cl}$ to form cyclophosphazines $(\ce{NPCl2})_n$ where $n \geq 3$. Write the balanced equation for the formation of cyclophosphazine with $n = 3$ and draw the structure of this product.

problems.title: Cobalt complexes
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (11 marks). Cobalt complexes

A pink solid compound ($\mathbf{A}$) has the formula $\ce{CoCl3*5NH3*H2O}$. An aqueous solution of this salt, which is also pink, on titration with $\ce{AgNO3}$ gives three moles of $\ce{AgCl}$ per mole of $\mathbf{A}$. Solid $\mathbf{A}$ on heating above $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gives a purple solid ($\mathbf{B}$) with the same ratio of $\ce{NH3}$:Cl. Compound $\mathbf{B}$ on titration with $\ce{AgNO3}$ gives two moles of $\ce{AgCl}$ per mole of $\mathbf{B}$.

7.1 (0.5 mark) Write the electronic configuration of cobalt in compound $\mathbf{A}$.

7.2 (1.5 marks) Write the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ with their IUPAC names.

7.3 (1.5 marks) Valence bond theory is useful in predicting shapes of complexes. Show the arrangement of the electrons for cobalt in the low spin purple complex $\mathbf{B}$. Predict the hybridization and the shape of this complex.

Although Valence bond theory is successful in predicting the shapes of complexes, it is unable to explain magnetic properties of coordination complexes. Crystal field theory (CFT) not only explains the magnetic properties but also accounts for color and spectra of these complexes. CFT is based on splitting of the d orbitals of the central metal in presence of ligands.

7.4 a) (1 mark) Using CFT draw the d orbital energy level diagram for the purple complex $\mathbf{B}$. Label the energy levels and show the electron distribution.

b) (0.5 mark) Complex $\mathbf{B}$ is (Mark X in the correct box)

• paramagnetic
• diamagnetic

7.5 (1.5 marks) Using CFT, show the arrangement of the electrons on the central metal atom in the complex ion $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]^{2+}}$. State with justification, whether $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]^{2+}}$ is readily oxidized or not.

7.6 (2 marks) For the complex $\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl3]}$, draw the structures of possible stereoisomers and label them with stereochemical descriptors.

7.7 (1 mark) A set of equivalent protons in a molecule gives one signal in the $^{1}\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum. The number of signal/s for the isomers drawn in 7.6 will be

7.8 (1.5 marks) Draw the structures of the following complexes and predict which one will be chiral.

a) cis $\ce{[CoCl2(ox)2]^{3-}}$

b) trans $\ce{[CoCl2(ox)2]^{3-}}$

where ox = oxalate ligand (represent the same as $\overset{\frown}{\mathrm{o\ \ o}}$ in the answer).

problems.title: Electrochemical cells
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (10 marks). Electrochemical cells

A secondary cell is one that can be recharged. Lead battery or the common car battery is an example of a secondary cell. Similarly, a battery using an alkali is known as the Edison cell. The Edison cell is represented as follows.

$$\mathrm{Fe(s)\ |\ FeO(s),\ 20\%\ KOH,\ Ni_2O_3(s),\ NiO(s)\ |\ Ni(s)}$$

8.1 (1 mark) Write the half cell reactions and overall cell reaction for the above cell.

8.2 (1 mark) If a student adds distilled water to the cell so that the concentration of $\ce{KOH}$ reduces to half of its original value, $E_\mathrm{cell}$ will (Mark X in the correct box)

(i) get doubled

(ii) be halved

(iii) remain unchanged

8.3 (4 marks) A student was asked to set up the following cell.

$$\begin{array}{l|l||l|l} \ce{Fe(s)} & \ce{Fe^{3+}(aq)} & \ce{Ag+(aq)} & \ce{Ag(s)} \\ & c = 0.05\,\mathrm{M} & c = 0.1\,\mathrm{M} & \end{array}$$

Calculate $E^0$ for this cell using the following data;

$E^0_{\ce{Fe^{3+}(aq), Fe^{2+}(aq)}} = 0.771\,\mathrm{V}$; $E^0_{\ce{Fe^{2+}(aq)/Fe(s)}} = -0.440\,\mathrm{V}$; $E^0_{\ce{Ag+(aq)/Ag(s)}} = 0.799\,\mathrm{V}$

Hence calculate $E_\mathrm{cell}$ at 298 K.

8.4 (1 mark) In a hurry, the student interchanged the electrodes, i.e. he placed the silver electrode in the solution of ferric ions (left hand half cell) and iron electrode in the solution of silver ions (right hand half cell). Write the reactions that may occur in each of the half cells due to this interchange.

8.5 (3 marks) Assuming that the reaction in the left hand half cell in 8.4 reaches equilibrium, calculate

(i) equilibrium constant for the reaction.

(ii) concentration of all the ions in the left hand half cell.

i) (0.5 mark) Is Quina a nylon or a polyester?

ii) (1 mark) Identify the monomers used to synthesize Quina.

9.3 (3 marks) Classify the following peptides as acidic, basic or neutral and state whether the charge on the peptide will be positive, negative or zero at pH = 6.0 (Refer to the table provided on page no.39).

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} & & \text{Nature} & & & \text{Charge} & \\ \text{Peptide} & \text{Acidic} & \text{Basic} & \text{Neutral} & \text{Positive} & \text{Negative} & \text{Zero} \\ \hline \text{Gly-Leu-Val} & & & & & & \\ \hline \text{Leu-Trp-Lys-Gly-Lys} & & & & & & \\ \hline \text{Arg-Ser-Val} & & & & & & \end{array}$$

9.4 a) (1.5 marks) For the following peptide give the products of complete hydrolysis

9.5 The artificial sweetener aspartame is a methyl ester of synthetic dipeptide Asp-Phe

i) (0.5 mark) How many stereoisomers of aspartame are possible?

ii) (1 mark) Draw the structure of aspartame.

Electrophoresis is a method for separation of a mixture of amino acids. In this method, a sample of an amino acid mixture is placed at the centre of a piece of filter paper or a gel. The paper or the gel is then placed in a buffered solution between two electrodes and an electric field is applied. Depending on the net charge, an amino acid will move either to the anode or to the cathode.

9.6 (1 mark) A mixture of arginine (pI=10.76), alanine (pI=6.02) and aspartic acid (pI=2.98) is separated by electrophoresis at pH = 5 (pI is the isoelectric point). Identify the amino acids $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in the chromatogram given below.

problems.title: Thermal and photolytic decomposition of Acetaldehyde
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 marks). Thermal and photolytic decomposition of Acetaldehyde

The stoichiometric equation for the pyrolysis of acetaldehyde to methane and carbon monoxide is as follows: $\ce{CH3CHO -> CH4 + CO}$

1.1 (a) (0.5 mark) The order of this reaction determined experimentally was 1.5. Write the rate equation for the reaction.

(b) (1 mark) If $v$ is the rate corresponding to $P_\mathrm{CH_3CHO} = P_1$, what is the (i) order and (ii) rate of reaction, when $P_\mathrm{CH_3CHO} = 4P_1$?

1.2 (1 mark) The pyrolysis of acetaldehyde under certain conditions, can be an intramolecular process. What products are formed in the pyrolysis of a mixture of $\ce{CH3CHO}$ and $\ce{CD3CDO}$?

1.3 The major steps in the gas phase thermal pyrolysis of acetaldehyde, as identified by Rice and Herzfeld are as follows

$$\begin{array}{lll} \ce{CH3CHO(g)} & \xrightarrow{k_1} {}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3(g)} + {}^{\bullet}\ce{CHO(g)} & \text{(i)} \\ {}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3(g)} + \ce{CH3CHO(g)} & \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{CH4(g)} + {}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3CO(g)} & \text{(ii)} \\ {}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3CO(g)} & \xrightarrow{k_3} {}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3(g)} + \ce{CO(g)} & \text{(iii)} \\ 2\,{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3(g)} & \xrightarrow{k_4} \ce{C2H6} & \text{(iv)} \end{array}$$

(a) (1 mark) Identify the propagation and termination steps from the above reactions.

(b) (2 marks) Assuming ${}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3}$ and ${}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3CO}$ to be under steady state (i.e. the rate of formation and rate of consumption of an intermediate species are equal), derive expressions for (i) $[{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3}]$ and (ii) $[{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3CO}]$ in terms of $[\ce{CH3CHO}]$.

(c) (1 mark) Deduce $\mathrm{d}[\ce{CO}]/\mathrm{d}t$ in terms of $[\ce{CH3CHO}]$.

1.4 (a) (1.5 marks) In the photochemical decomposition of acetaldehyde, one photon of absorbed light decomposes one molecule of $\ce{CH3CHO}$ into ${}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3}$ and ${}^{\bullet}\ce{CHO}$. If '$I_\mathrm{abs}$' is the intensity of light absorbed in the reaction,

(i) Write the rate equation for this photochemical decomposition. (Note: the first step in the photochemical reaction is temperature independent)

(ii) Calculate $[{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3}]$ and $\mathrm{d}[\ce{CO}]/\mathrm{d}t$ assuming steps (ii) to (iv) given in 1.3 are same and $[{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3}]$, $[{}^{\bullet}\ce{CH3CO}]$ are under steady state.

(b) (1 mark) If C-C, C-H, and C=O bond energies in acetaldehyde are 377, 421 and $720\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively, calculate the wavelength of radiation (in nm) required to bring about the photochemical decomposition of acetaldehyde.

1.5 The Arrhenius (pre exponential) factors and activation energy values for steps (i) to (iv) in 1.3 are $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ and $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$ and $E_4$ respectively.

(a) (1.5 marks) Calculate the overall activation energy $E_\mathrm{thermal}$ for the thermal decomposition of acetaldehyde.

(b) (1 mark) Write the expression for overall activation energy, $E_\mathrm{photochemical}$ of photochemical decomposition of acetaldehyde.

1.6 The recombination of methyl radicals has no activation barrier. The activation energy values for the first step in the thermal decomposition of acetaldehyde in (1.3) and $E_\mathrm{photochemical}$ are $309.32\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $41.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively.

(a) (1 mark) Calculate the overall activation energy for the thermal decomposition of acetaldehyde

(b) (2 marks) Calculate the rate constant and rate of overall reaction for the thermal decomposition of acetaldehyde at 101 kPa and 800 K, if overall Arrhenius factor is $2.3\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{dm^{3/2}\,mol^{-1/2}\,sec^{-1}}$.

1.7 $\ce{CH3CHO}$ can be formed from $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$ and further get oxidised to $\ce{CH3COOH}$ as

$$\ce{CH3CH2OH} \xrightarrow{k_5} \ce{CH3CHO} \xrightarrow{k_6} \ce{CH3COOH}$$

(a) (1.5 marks) Qualitatively sketch the concentration vs time plots of $\ce{CH3CHO}$, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$ and $\ce{CH3COOH}$, till the reaction goes to completion.

(b) (1 mark) If both the reactions in 1.7 are of 1st order, $[\ce{CH3CHO}]$ is related to initial concentration of alcohol $[\ce{CH3CH2OH}]_0$ by the equation,

$$\frac{[\ce{CH3CHO}]}{[\ce{CH3CH2OH}]_0} = \frac{k_5}{k_6 - k_5}\left(e^{-k_5 t} - e^{-k_6 t}\right)$$

Derive the expression for $[\ce{CH3CHO}]$ in terms of $[\ce{CH3CH2OH}]$ if $k_5 \ll k_6$.

The two d-orbitals then have different energies. This is known as Jahn Teller distortion. This distortion usually occurs by elongation or contraction along z-axis, and the single electron correspondingly occupies highest energy $\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ or $\mathrm{d}_{z^2}$ orbital. In a crystal lattice structure of $\ce{CuF2}$, the $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ is six coordinate with four $\ce{F^-}$ at a distance of $1.93\,\text{Å}$ and two $\ce{F^-}$ at $2.27\,\text{Å}$. ii) $\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital.

The structure of benzene puzzled chemists for a longtime after its discovery in 1825. Some of the structures proposed for benzene are highly strained cyclic compounds. In one second, each cylinder goes through 25 burn cycles and consumes 0.400 g of fuel. The compression ratio, which is the ratio between the smallest and largest volume within the cylinder as the piston moves forward and backward is 1:8.

6.6 (3 marks) Calculate the air intake of the engine ($\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$), if the gaseous fuel and air are introduced into the cylinder when its volume is largest until the pressure is 101.0 kPa. The temperature of both incoming air and fuel is $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (Assume the fuel to be isooctane, $\ce{C8H18}$)

Air contains 21.0 % of $\ce{O2}$ and 79.0 % of $\ce{N2}$ (by volume). It is assumed that 10.0 % of the carbon of the fuel forms CO upon combustion and that $\ce{N2}$ in air remains inert.

6.7 (2.5 marks) The gasified fuel and air are compressed to their lowest volume and then ignited.

The overall stoichiometric equation for the combustion reaction is

$$\ce{C8H18 + 12.1 O2 -> 0.8 CO + 7.2 CO2 + 9 H2O}$$

Calculate the temperatures of the

i) gases just at the time of maximum compression, and

ii) exhaust gases leaving the cylinder if the final pressure in the cylinder is 200 kpa.

Relevant data needed for one burn cycle is given below:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{Compound} & \Delta H_\mathrm{f}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & C_p\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & \begin{array}{l}\textbf{Composition of gases after} \\ \textbf{combustion}\ (\mathrm{Mol}\times10^{-4})\end{array} \\ \hline \ce{N2(g)} & 0.0 & 29.13 & 101.91 \\ \hline \ce{O2(g)} & 0.0 & 29.36 & 10.10 \\ \hline \ce{CO(g)} & -110.53 & 29.14 & 1.12 \\ \hline \ce{CO2(g)} & -395.51 & 37.11 & 10.11 \\ \hline \ce{H2O(g)} & -241.82 & 33.58 & 12.36 \\ \hline \text{Isooctane} & -187.82 & & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

6.8 (3.5 marks) To convert $\ce{CO(g)}$ into $\ce{CO2(g)}$ the exhaust gases are led through a bed of catalysts with the following work function:

$$\left(\frac{n(\mathrm{CO})}{n(\mathrm{CO_2})}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\times k\left(\frac{n(\mathrm{CO})}{n(\mathrm{CO_2})}\right)_\mathrm{i} \times v \times e^{-\left(T/T_0\right)}$$

where, $[n(\mathrm{CO}) / n(\mathrm{CO_2})]$ is the molar ratio of CO and $\ce{CO2}$ leaving the catalyst bed, $[n(\mathrm{CO}) / n(\mathrm{CO_2})]_\mathrm{i}$ is the molar ratio before entering the catalyst bed, $v$ is the flow rate in $\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$ and $T$ the temperature of the exhaust gases. $T_0$ is a reference temperature (373 K) and $k$ is $3.141\,\mathrm{s\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate the molar composition of the exhaust gases leaving the catalyst bed.

problems.title: [Acetic acid in vinegar]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (10 marks). [Acetic acid in vinegar]

Vinegar is an acid with its key ingredient, acetic acid. It is widely used for food preservation and cooking. The acetic acid concentration for table vinegar is typically 5% whereas higher concentration upto 18% is used as preservative. The word "vinegar" is derived from vin aigre, meaning "sour wine".

A table vinegar sample contains 5% (mass/mass) of acetic acid.

7.1 (1 mark) To what volume 10 mL of the above sample should be diluted to prepare 0.10 M acetic acid solution. (density $1.05\,\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}$, Molar mass of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ – $60.0\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$)

7.2 (1 mark) Write balanced equation for the dissociation of acetic acid $[\ce{CH3COOH}]$ in the above solution and give an appropriate expression for equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{a}$.

7.3 (1.5 marks) For the diluted solution, write the appropriate expression for total concentration of acetic acid expressed as $C_\mathrm{T}$. Derive the exact expression for $[\ce{H3O+}]$ in terms of $K_\mathrm{a}$ and $C_\mathrm{T}$.

7.4 (1.5 marks) Apply appropriate approximation to simplify the expression for $[\ce{H3O+}]$ written by you in 7.3 and calculate the pH of the diluted vinegar solution. ($K_\mathrm{a} = 1.75\times10^{-5}$)

7.5 (4 marks) 5.0 mL of 0.1 M NaOH solution is added to 50 mL of the 0.1 M acetic acid solution

a) Write the equilibrium reactions for dissociated and undissociated acetic acid present in the above solution.

b) For the above system, write appropriate expressions for $[\ce{CH3COOH}]_\mathrm{eq}$ and $[\ce{CH3COO^-}]_\mathrm{eq}$. (hint: the expressions should have $[\ce{H3O+}]$, $[\ce{OH^-}]$, $C_\mathrm{T}$ and $[\ce{CH3COONa}]$).

c) Apply appropriate approximation and get the simplified expression for $[\ce{H3O+}]$.

d) Calculate the pH of the resulting acetic acid solution

7.6 (1 mark) Calculate the pH when 50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH is added to 50 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid solution. ($K_\mathrm{w} = 1.00\times10^{-14}$)

problems.title: [Chromium: Latimer diagram, electrochemistry and analysis]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 marks). [Chromium: Latimer diagram, electrochemistry and analysis]

Chromium, the first element in Group 6 is a steely-gray, lustrous, hard metal. The name of this element is derived from the Greek word chrōma meaning colour because many of its compounds are intensely coloured. This element was discovered by Louis Nicolas Vauquelin in the mineral crocoite (lead chromate).

The diagram indicating the standard potential values connecting species of an element present in different oxidation states is known as Latimer diagram. In such a diagram, the most oxidized form of an element is represented at the extreme left, and in successive species the oxidation number of the element goes on decreasing from left to right. The numerical values of $E^\circ$ (volt) are written above the lines joining the successive species. Latimer diagram for chromium is presented below. (All data refer to pH = 1)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-1-fig1.png

1.1 (1.5 marks) Calculate the values of X and Y in the above Latimer diagram.

1.2 (2 marks) With appropriate calculations, show Cr (IV) disproportionate to Cr (III) and Cr (VI).

1.3 (0.5 mark) $[\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}]/[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]$ system is used as an oxidising agent. Write the balanced chemical equation for this half cell reaction.

1.4 (2 marks) Calculate the change in the potential of the above system, if the pH is changed from 1 to 3 ($T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$) ($E^\circ(\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}/\ce{Cr^{3+}}) = 1.33\,\mathrm{V}$. (Note: With change in pH in this range, assume that $[\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}]$ and $[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]$ practically remain constant).

1.5 (2.5 marks) $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1N potassium dichromate is titrated with 0.1N Fe(II) solution. Calculate the potential of the system when $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1N Fe(II) is added. (pH = 1, $E^\circ = \ce{Fe^{3+}}/\ce{Fe^{2+}} = 0.77\,\mathrm{V}$)

In Chrome plating, a layer of chromium is electroplated on a metal object. In this process, chromium trioxide ($\ce{CrO3}$) is used as the source of chromium. In a typical setup, an electrolytic cell was filled with 150 L solution containing chromium trioxide (in this solution, chromium trioxide exists as chromic acid $\ce{H2CrO4}$). The electrolysis was carried out for 8 hrs with a current of 2000 A. The object that acted as cathode gained 350 g of chromium at the end of 8 hrs. At cathode, in addition to deposition of chromium, another reaction involving liberation of a gas also took place. Hence, the efficiency for the electrodeposition of chromium was less than 100%.

1.6 (2.5 marks) Write balanced equation for the half cell reaction resulting in deposition of chromium at the cathode. Using this equation and the given data, calculate the percent efficiency for the electrodeposition of metallic chromium.

1.7 (3 marks) Write balanced chemical equations for the half cell reactions involving liberation of gases at cathode and anode respectively. Using these equations, calculate the volume of the gases liberated at the cathode and the anode ($T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$ and $P = 1.013\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/m^2}$).

1.8 (3 marks) An insecticide formulation contains copper (II) oleate $\ce{Cu(C18H33O2)2}$ (Molar mass = 626). A 9.9 g sample of the insecticide preparation was wet-ashed with a sulfuric-nitric acid mixture to destroy its organic components. The copper in the sample was then precipitated as the basic chromate, $\ce{CuCrO4.2CuO.2H2O}$, with an excess of potassium chromate. The solid was filtered, washed free of excess reagent, and then redissolved in acid:

$$\ce{2(CuCrO4.2CuO.2H2O) (s) + 10 H+ (aq.) -> 6 Cu^{2+} (aq.) + Cr2O7^{2-} (aq.) + 9 H2O}$$

Titration of the liberated dichromate required 15.7 mL of 0.232 M $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$. Calculate the percentage of copper (II) oleate in the sample.

problems.title: [Group 13 oxides, boranes and carboranes]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (11 marks). [Group 13 oxides, boranes and carboranes]

Most elements form oxides and hydroxides with different characteristics. Often, regular periodic trends are observed in these oxides and hydroxides. Hydroxides of Na and Mg are distinctly alkaline, while oxides of N and S are distinctly acidic.

2.1 (1.5 marks) Identify the nature of the following oxides of Group 13 elements:- (strike off whichever is not correct)

$$\begin{array}{lllll} \ce{B2O3} & \text{acidic} & \text{basic} & \text{amphoteric} & \text{neutral} \\ \ce{Al2O3} & \text{acidic} & \text{basic} & \text{amphoteric} & \text{neutral} \\ \ce{Tl2O3} & \text{acidic} & \text{basic} & \text{amphoteric} & \text{neutral} \end{array}$$

Boron the first member of group 13, forms a hydride $\ce{BH3}$. This hydride exists as a dimer ($\ce{B2H6}$).

2.2 (0.5 mark) Draw the structure of $\ce{B2H6}$.

(0.5 mark) The unusual bond present in $\ce{B2H6}$ is a -

a) Two centered $3\mathrm{e^-}$ bond

b) Three centered $2\mathrm{e^-}$ bond

c) Four centered $2\mathrm{e^-}$ bond

d) Four centered $4\mathrm{e^-}$ bond

2.3 (1.5 marks) Diborane reacts violently with water and releases hydrogen. Write a balanced equation of this reaction.

A variety of polymeric boranes and anionic boron hydrides are formed. Closo-boranes are the compounds having formula $\ce{B_{n}H_{n}^{2-}}$. They have closed regular polyhedral frameworks of boron atoms, with each boron bound to the neighbouring boron atoms and a terminal hydrogen atom. An example is $\ce{B6H6^{2-}}$ which has the following structure ($\mathbf{X}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-2-fig1.png

A neutral nido-borane ($\mathbf{Y}$) is formed by removing an apical Boron atom from $\mathbf{X}$ and adding the requisite number of hydrogens.

2.4 (2 marks) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Y}$.

The corresponding arachno-boranes are formed by removal of two neighbouring apical boron atoms in $\mathbf{X}$.

2.5 (0.5 mark) Write the general formula of arachano-boranes.

2.6 (2 marks) Draw the structures of the possible arachano-boranes derived from $\mathbf{X}$.

Carboranes are neutral compounds which are formed by isoelectronic replacement of Boron by Carbon in boranes.

2.7 (0.5 mark) Write the molecular formula of a carborane ($\mathbf{Z}$) obtained by replacing two Boron by carbon atoms in closo-dodecaborane anions.

2.8 (2 marks) Draw the structures of all possible isomers of $\mathbf{Z}$ (show only boron-carbon framework).

problems.title: Thermodynamics of a sustainable bio process
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (18 marks). Thermodynamics of a sustainable bio process

A. Photosynthesis is a bio process by which plants make energy rich molecules from low energy molecules with the help of energy from sun light. The photosynthesis of glucose can be represented as

$$\ce{6CO2 (g) + 6H2O (g)} + h\nu \ce{-> C6H12O6 (s) + 6O2 (g)} \qquad (1)$$

The energy of one mole of a photon of wave length $\lambda$ is known as one Einstein.

3.1 (1.5 marks) 48 Einsteins of 650 nm are absorbed by a plant for the production of 1 mole of glucose as given in (1). Calculate the % efficiency for the production of glucose by photosynthesis. The energy required for the formation of 1 mole of glucose is 2870 kJ.

3.2 (1.5 marks) On an average, solar radiation produces $7\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{kg}$ of glucose annually on earth. Calculate the annual decrease in the $\ce{CO2}$ level in the troposphere in ppm, due to photosynthesis. (1 ppm = 1 g of $\ce{CO2}$ per $10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}$ of air in troposphere). Assume that the total mass of air envelope surrounding the earth is $5.0\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and 80% of it is present in the troposphere.

3.3 (1.5 marks) Heats of combustion of graphite and hydrogen at 298 K are $-393.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $-285.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively. If on combustion 1 g of glucose releases 15.58 kJ of energy, calculate the heat of formation of glucose at 298 K.

Diabetic patients have to monitor their blood glucose level periodically. Home glucometer is an appliance used for this purpose. This device consists of a disposable test strip with carbon working electrodes and a reference electrode. The working electrode is covered with the enzyme glucose oxidase, which catalyses the reaction of glucose with dissolved oxygen.

3.4 (0.5 mark) Write balanced equation for the reaction of glucose with $\ce{O2}$ in which $\ce{O2}$ is converted to $\ce{H2O2}$.

The $\ce{H2O2}$ generated is oxidized at the second working electrode generating a current, which is proportional to the glucose present in the sample. Typically, 5 mmoles of glucose produces 2.5 mA current.

3.5 (1.5 marks) A weight lifter lifts a weight of 160 kg through a height of 2.4 m. Assuming all the energy required for this task is obtained by the combustion of glucose, calculate the change in the current produced by a sample of blood of the weight lifter. Same volume of blood (5 mL) is tested both before and after lifting the weight and the total volume of blood in his body is 5 L. (1 g of glucose releases 15.58 kJ of energy)

Electrochemical oxidation of glucose to $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$, which is the reverse of photosynthesis, is an important reaction and it can be used in the construction of a fuel cell. In a fuel cell, a working substance called fuel is electrochemically oxidised by $\ce{O2}$. A fuel cell was devised with glucose under suitable pH conditions.

3.6 (1.5 marks) Write balanced equations for the half cell reactions corresponding to oxidation of glucose.

3.7 (1 mark) Calculate the emf of this fuel cell at 25 °C if $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ of photosynthesis are $2.82\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ and $-182\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively.

3.8 (1 mark) Variation of emf of an electrochemical cell with temperature is known as the temperature coefficient of the cell. If $\delta(\Delta G/\delta T)_P = -\Delta S$, calculate the temperature coefficient of the glucose fuel cell at 25 °C from the data given in 3.7.

3.9 (2 marks) A glucose fuel cell was designed to generate 4000 Watts which was used to heat a room of 5 m × 5 m × 3 m dimensions. The room is perfectly insulated and no heat flows out of the room. Calculate the time needed to increase the temperature of the room by 20 °C, if the room was initially at 10 °C and 1 atm. pressure. Assume that the air in the room behaves like an ideal gas and its molar heat capacity is $2.5R$.

B. In photosynthesis, the Sun,(S) the Earth (E) and the Photosynthetic Organism (PO) can be considered as three different thermodynamic systems. The sun and the earth are at a constant temperature ($T_\mathrm{S} = 5762\,\mathrm{K}$; $T_\mathrm{E} = 298.15\,\mathrm{K}$) at constant pressure, volume and composition. The photosynthetic organism has a constant volume, temperature and pressure and $T_\mathrm{PO} = T_\mathrm{E}$.

The photosynthetic process is of three steps as shown

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-3-fig1.png

3.10 (1 mark) Write the expressions for $\mathrm{d}U_\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{d}G_\mathrm{S}$ for step1 in terms of $T_\mathrm{S}$ where U and G are internal energy and Gibbs free energy and S refers to the sun.

Efficient plants need 60 photons to synthesize one glucose molecule.

3.11 (1 mark) Write the expression for the change in the internal energy of the sun $(\Delta U)_\mathrm{S}$ and that of PO $(\Delta U)_\mathrm{PO}$ in step (1) if the wave length of the absorbed photons is $\lambda$.

3.12 (1 mark) What is the expression for the total entropy change of step 1, $(\Delta S)_\mathrm{step1}$?

In step (2), PO uses part of the energy absorbed in step (1) and transforms this into chemical energy in the synthesis of glucose. In this step PO dose not exchange energy with its surroundings.

3.13 (1 mark) What is the total entropy change in step 2, $(\Delta S)_\mathrm{step2}$ in terms of $\Delta G_\mathrm{PO}$?

In step (3), PO transmits to the earth the remaining energy that was not used in the synthesis of glucose.

3.14 (1 mark) Show that $\Delta S_\mathrm{step3} = 0$

$T_\mathrm{S}$ is very high and $1/T_\mathrm{S}$ can be approximated to zero.

3.15 (1 mark) Under this condition, write the expression for the overall entropy change of Scheme 1.

problems.title: Organosulphur Compounds

Problem 4 (23 marks). Organosulphur Compounds

Organosulphur reagents are useful in part due to the capacity of sulphur to utilize third shell orbitals for bonding besides its ability to occur in valence states higher than 2.

4.1 (1 mark) Draw the Lewis structure of thiosulphate ion ($\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$).

Sulphur ylides are compounds in which positively charged sulphur is bonded to a negatively charged carbon atom (carbanion). Sulphur ylides are useful intermediates in synthesis.

problems.title: [Chemistry of main group, d- and f-block elements]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (17 marks). [Chemistry of main group, d- and f-block elements]

A. Chemistry of Main Group Elements

Shapes of molecules containing a central p-block atom tend to be controlled by the number of electrons in the valence shell of the central atom. The valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR) provides a simple approach for predicting the shapes of such species.

5.1 a) (0.5 mark) Draw the Lewis structure of $\ce{ClF3}$ on the basis of VSEPR.

b) (1 mark) Lone pairs of electrons in the valence shell of the central atom in a molecule can occupy different positions. Draw all the possible structure/s of $\ce{ClF3}$.

c) (0.5 mark) State the most stable shape that is predicted by the VSEPR model.

5.2 Shape of triatomic molecules like $\ce{SO2}$ [O=S=O] can be explained on the basis of hybridization.

a) (2 marks) Give box structure diagrams of S atom in the ground, excited and hybridized states.

b) (0.5 mark) Draw the shape of $\ce{SO2}$ molecule

c) (0.5 mark) Do the electron pairs involved in $\pi$-bonds affect the shape of the molecule?

• Yes

• No

A number of compounds of p-block elements are routinely used as reducing or oxidizing agents. Compounds of the last two elements of Group 14 (C group), Sn and Pb, are both oxidizing and reducing agents. $\ce{Sn^{2+}}$ compounds like $\ce{SnO}$ and $\ce{SnCl2}$ are well known reducing agents, while $\ce{PbO2}$ acts as an oxidizing agent.

5.3 i) (1 mark) Based on the above observations mark the correct statement

a) $\ce{Sn^{2+}}$ is more stable than $\ce{Sn^{4+}}$

b) $\ce{Sn^{4+}}$ is more stable than $\ce{Sn^{2+}}$

c) $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ is more stable than $\ce{Pb^{4+}}$

d) $\ce{Pb^{4+}}$ is more stable than $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$

ii) (0.5 mark) Sodium bismuthate, ($\ce{NaBiO3}$), is expected to behave as a -

• oxidizing agent

• reducing agent

iii) (2 marks) In an alkaline medium, manganese chloride reacts with sodium borate. Complete the following chemical equation for this redox reaction.

$$\ce{MnCl2 + NaBiO3 -> NaCl} + \underline{\qquad\qquad} + \underline{\qquad\qquad}$$

B. Chemistry of d and f- block elements

5.4 (4 marks) Complexes of iron exist with different numbers of unpaired electrons. For the given complexes, write the number of unpaired electrons and state whether they are high spin or low spin species.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Complex} & \text{No of unpaired electrons} & \text{Spin state} \\ \hline \ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}} & & \\ \hline \ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{3-}} & & \\ \hline \ce{[FeCl4]^{-}} & & \\ \hline \ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^{2+}} & & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

5.5 (0.5 mark) The oxygen taken during respiration in human beings is carried through the blood stream with the help of haemoglobin. The latter is a tetramer containing four heme (iron-porphyrin) units. The oxidation state of iron in deoxyhaemoglobin is +2 and it is a high spin paramagnetic species. On binding with oxygen, the iron in haemoglobin changes its coordination sphere from 5 to 6. This results in the change in magnetic property. The value of magnetic moment in each unit of oxyhaemoglobin is

5.6 i) (1 mark) $\ce{[IrCl6]^{2-}}$ is a low spin octahedral complex, this is because

a) the central metal ion is in higher oxidation state.

b) Ir belongs to third transition series.

c) $\ce{Cl-}$, despite being a weak ligand, in this case acts as a strong ligand.

d) it is a complex anion with −2 charge.

ii) (1 mark) Draw a simple labeled crystal field splitting diagram for $\ce{[IrCl6]^{2-}}$ showing distribution of electrons in the split d-orbitals.

The f-block elements, lanthanides and actinides, are characterized by gradual filling of the 4f and 5f sub-shell respectively.

5.7 (2 marks) The most common oxidation state of lanthanides is 3+. This oxidation state of lanthanide ions arises due to the loss of two 6s electrons and one 5d electron in 4f/5d orbital. Besides 3+, some lanthanides like Ce, Sm and Eu also show other oxidation states.

Give the chemical equations for the general reactions of lanthanides (Ln) with i) water and ii) acid, and of cerium (Ce) with iii) oxygen and iv) fluorine.

problems.title: Chemistry of unusual organic compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (16 marks). Chemistry of unusual organic compounds

Organic chemists have synthesized many compounds having unusual properties. Compounds having molecules which are apparently highly strained have also been synthesized in the laboratory. Many times the compounds have been named by chemists, taking into account the resemblance of the molecules with well known objects around us like basketane, pagodane, penguinone, garudane.

Sumanene ($\mathbf{4}$), (Sanskrit suman = flower) is one such compound, whose molecule has a flower like shape. Synthesis of $\mathbf{4}$ starts with a simple bicyclic compound norbornadiene ($\mathbf{1}$). Conceptual trimerization of $\mathbf{1}$ yields the crucial intermediate $\mathbf{2}$ ($\ce{C21H18}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-6-fig1.png

6.1 (1.5 marks) Draw the structure of two possible stereoisomers of $\mathbf{2}$.

$\mathbf{2}$ undergoes a rearrangement in the presence of a Ru-catalyst to form a precursor $\mathbf{3}$ of sumanene. $\mathbf{3}$ on oxidation with a suitable reagent gives $\mathbf{4}$.

6.2 (1 mark) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{3}$.

$\mathbf{4}$ on oxidation with alkaline $\ce{KMnO4}$ gives $\mathbf{5}$.

6.3 (1 mark) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{5}$ ($\ce{C21H6O3}$).

Cubane ($\mathbf{10}$) is another interesting strained molecule. It is prepared through a reaction sequence with following intermediates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-6-fig2.png

(i) carbonyl group ($\mathbf{b}$) has conjugated double bond

(ii) carbonyl group ($\mathbf{a}$) is sterically less hindered

(iii) carbonyl group ($\mathbf{b}$) is sterically less hindered

(iv) the double bond adjacent to carbonyl group ($\mathbf{a}$) assists the reaction

$\mathbf{6}$ is obtained by dimerization of $\mathbf{X}$ through Diels – Alder reaction. $\mathbf{X}$ is obtained from cyclopentanone ($\mathbf{11}$) as shown below.

6.5 (3.5 marks) Draw the structures of the intermediates ($\mathbf{12}$-$\mathbf{15}$) and $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-6-fig3.png

$^{**}$ NBS is a reagent used to selectively brominate the allylic carbon.

Favorskii rearrangement is a base catalysed reaction of $\alpha$–haloketone to a carboxylic acid as shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2011-6-fig4.png

In the cubane synthesis conversion of $\mathbf{8} \rightarrow \mathbf{9}$ involves a Favorskii rearrangement.

6.6 (1 mark) Draw the structure of the neutral intermediate formed in the conversion of $\mathbf{8} \rightarrow \mathbf{9}$.

Cubane on chlorination gives dichlorocubane.

6.7 (1.5 marks) Draw the structures of all isomeric dichlorocubanes.

6.8 (1 mark) Cubane is a $\underline{\qquad\qquad}$

(i) tetracyclic compound

(ii) pentacyclic compound

(iii) hexacyclic compound

(iv) octacyclic compound

Like cubane, propellane ($\ce{C5H6}$) is another fascinating strained molecule, which can be synthesized from a carbene intermediate.

problems.problem:
Problem 2 (12 marks). Analysis of alloys

Alloys are materials with specific properties that are obtained by combination of different metals in definite proportions. Both conventional and modern techniques are used for the determination of the chemical composition of an alloy. This question deals with different methods that are used to determine the composition of a copper-zinc-lead alloy.

A.

Iodometric method is one of the conventional methods used for the estimation of copper content of an alloy. In this method, the alloy sample is first dissolved in nitric acid, evaporated to dryness and then extracted with dilute sulphuric acid. In one such analysis, 0.685 g of an alloy sample was treated with acid and diluted to 250 mL (solution A). 10 mL of solution A was used for the estimation of copper iodometrically. For this titration, an excess of solid potassium iodide was added to 10 mL of solution A which was preadjusted to an optimum pH. The liberated $\ce{I2}$ was titrated with sodium thiosulphate solution.

2.1 (1.5 marks) Write the balanced equations of the reactions involved in

i) reaction of Cu(II) with iodide and

ii) the titration.

2.2 (1.5 marks) The volume of thiosulphate required for the titration was 6.1 mL. The strength of supplied aqueous thiosulphate solution was expected to be 0.05 M. Calculate the amount of copper in grams and the percentage of copper in the alloy sample.

However, thiosulphate is not a primary standard and needs to be standardized to know its exact molarity. The above thiosulphate solution was standardized using 0.0125 M potassium dichromate solution. For this purpose, excess of solid potassium iodide was added to 10 mL of potassium dichromate solution in an acidic medium and the liberated iodine was titrated with the thiosulphate solution.

2.3 (1 mark) Write the balanced equation of the reaction between dichromate and iodide.

2.4 (1 mark) The observed reading in the above titration was 15.5 mL. Calculate the exact molarity of the thiosulphate solution.

2.5 (1 mark) Using the molarity calculated by you, recalculate the amount of copper in grams present in the alloy sample. Calculate the relative percentage deviation for the copper content obtained in 2.2.

B.

Another method used to analyze a copper-zinc-lead alloy is electrolysis. In this method, the alloy sample is dissolved in nitric acid of suitable strength. In the presence of nitric acid, the lead present in the alloy is quantitatively oxidized to lead dioxide and deposited on the anode. In the process, the nitrate ions are reduced to $\ce{NH4+}$ which prevents liberation of hydrogen at the cathode.

2.6 (1 mark) Write the balanced equation for the reaction representing the reduction of nitrate ions to ammonium ions.

2.7 (0.5 mark) Write balanced equation of the reaction of formation of $\ce{PbO2}$ at the anode.

0.685g of copper-lead-zinc alloy containing 1% lead [w/w] was dissolved in nitric acid and diluted to $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ [solution B]. 100 mL of solution B was electrolyzed with a current of 1.47 mA for 1 hour and 20 minutes. This ensured that lead was completely converted to dioxide.

2.8 (1 mark) Calculate the millimoles of lead dioxide formed.

2.9 (1 mark) Calculate the fraction of the total current passed that is used in the formation of $\ce{PbO2}$.

C.

The zinc content in the alloy can be determined by an instrumental technique called Fluorimetry. This technique is based on the measurement of the intensity of the fluorescent radiation produced, which is directly proportional to the concentration of the species producing fluorescence. The reagent that is used for the determination of zinc by flourimetry is oxine. By itself, it does not show fluorescence, whereas zinc-oxine complex shows fluorescence. In such determinations fluorescence of the sample solution is measured first and then a standard zinc solution of known concentration is added to a definite volume of the sample solution. The fluorescence of the resulting solution is then measured. This technique is known as standard addition method.

2.10 (2.5 marks) The solution in 2.8, after the electrolysis (that is, after deposition of $\ce{PbO2}$) was evaporated to dryness and extracted with dil. sulphuric acid and diluted to 100 mL (solution C). 10 mL of solution C was further diluted to 100 mL (solution D). 1.0 mL of solution D was used for the fluorimetric determination of zinc. The data obtained is presented below,

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Vol of sample} & \text{Vol of oxine} & \text{Vol of 1ppm} & \text{Total volume} & \text{Fluorescence} \\ \text{solution } \mathbf{D}\ \text{(mL)} & \text{solution added (mL)} & \text{Zn added (mL)} & \text{in mL} & \text{intensity} \\ \hline 1.0 & 0.5 & \text{------} & 50 & 25 \\ \hline 1.0 & 0.5 & 1.0 & 50 & 42 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

From this data, calculate the amount of zinc in whole of Solution B, (2.8) and the percentage of zinc in the alloy sample.

A. Many chemical reactions can be brought about by the absorption of light of suitable wavelength. Such reactions are known as photochemical reactions. In a photochemical reaction, only the first step is photochemical and the rest are thermal. The energy of the absorbed photon is used for the chemical conversions.

For the photochemical combination of hydrogen and chlorine to form hydrogen chloride, the following mechanism was suggested.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Cl2} \xrightarrow{(h\nu)} 2\,\ce{Cl}^{\bullet} & \text{(i)} \\ \ce{Cl}^{\bullet} + \ce{H2} \xrightarrow{k_1} \ce{HCl} + \ce{H}^{\bullet} & \text{(ii)} \\ \ce{H}^{\bullet} + \ce{Cl2} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{HCl} + \ce{Cl}^{\bullet} & \text{(iii)} \\ 2\,\ce{Cl}^{\bullet} \xrightarrow{k_3} \ce{Cl2} & \text{(iv)} \end{array}$$

To simplify complex rate equations, one of the approximation methods used is steady state approximation. According to this concept, if a reaction involves a highly reactive intermediate ‘X’, after a short span of time, ‘X’ reaches a ‘steady state’. Under steady state, the rate of formation of X = rate of consumption of X. It is called as steady state because concentration of X remains constant at steady state.

In the above photochemical reaction, one photon of absorbed light converts one molecule of $\ce{Cl2}$ to Cl radicals. This step is temperature independent and hence the rate of this step depends only on the intensity of light absorbed, $I_\mathrm{abs}$.

A heat engine is a system that converts heat into mechanical work. A heat "source" generates thermal energy that brings a working substance to a high temperature. Problem 1 (17 marks). Metallurgy

Metallurgy is the technology of obtaining metals from their ores. Depending on the metal and the ore involved, metallurgical operations are divided into three broad divisions as hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy and electrometallurgy.

In hydrometallurgy, the metal is extracted into an aqueous solution using oxygen and a complexing agent. Hydrometallurgy is used for noble metals like silver and gold. The process is known as leaching. Potassium cyanide is traditionally used for extraction of gold.

In presence of air, native gold dissolves in a solution containing cyanide ions $\ce{(CN)^{-1}}$ forming $\ce{[Au(CN)2]^{-1}}$.

1.1 Write a balanced equation to represent dissolution of gold in KCN solution. (0.5 mark)

1.2 Calculate the mass of KCN required to extract gold from 100 kg of a rock sample having 2.2% gold on w/w basis. (1 mark)

Silver and gold both form cyanide complexes $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]^{-1}}$, $\ce{[Au(CN)2]^{-1}}$ with formation constants as $4.2\times10^{20}$ and $1.0\times10^{37}$ respectively.

1.3 Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction.

$$\ce{Au^{+1}(aq) + [Ag(CN)2]^{-1}(aq) <=> Ag^{+1}(aq) + [Au(CN)2]^{-1}(aq)}$$

(0.5 mark)

1.4 Using 1.3 and the information given below, calculate the equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{[Au(CN)2]^{-1}}$ and $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]^{-1}}$ when solid gold is added in excess to $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]^{-1}}$ solution. (under standard condition of temperature and pressure)

1) $\ce{Ag^{+1}(aq) + e- <=> Ag(s)}$ $\quad E^0 = 0.8\,\mathrm{V}$

2) $\ce{Au+(aq) + e- <=> Au(s)}$ $\quad E^0 = 1.83\,\mathrm{V}$

(2 marks)

Aqua regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and nitric acid in the ratio of 3:1 on volume basis. It was developed by the alchemists to dissolve gold. In the dissolution process, gold is oxidized and converted to a chloro complex and nitric acid gets reduced to nitrogen dioxide.

1.5 Write a balanced equation for the individual reactions. (1 mark)

In pyro-metallurgy the metals are extracted from ores and concentrates by heat treatment. This involves conversion to metal oxide. This is followed by the reduction of the oxide to the metal using carbon or carbon monoxide. Metals like iron, copper, zinc and manganese are obtained by this technique.

Ellingham diagram is a graph showing the variation of the standard free energy of formation ($\Delta G^\circ$) of metal oxides with temperature. The diagram also shows lines for formation of CO and $\ce{CO2}$.

b) $\Delta G = \Delta H + T\Delta S$

d) $\Delta G^0 = \Delta H^0 + T\Delta S^0$

ii) The statement that is true for the line $\ce{C -> CO2}$ is

b) the standard entropy change of the above reaction is negative

iii) The statement that is true for the line $\ce{CO -> CO2}$ is
a) the standard entropy change of the above reaction is positive

c) the standard entropy change of the above reaction is zero.

a) below $2200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
b) above $2500\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
c) not possible at any temperature

(4.5 marks)

In electrometallurgy, the pure metal is obtained by electrolysis of its appropriate salt. Aluminum is produced from bauxite by electro-reduction of alumina. The process is known as Hall- Herault’s process Alumina is dissolved in a conducting medium like cryolite $\ce{Na3AlF6}$, as it cannot conduct electricity in the molten state. problems.title: Energy storage devices
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (15 marks). Energy storage devices

A. Hydrogen storage as metal hydrides

Hydrogen is a renewable source of energy and considered as a fuel of the future. One of the problems of its use is storage and transportation. Research has shown that several metal hydrides act as ‘hydrogen tanks’. Large quantities of hydrogen can be absorbed on them and desorbed when needed through absorption/desorption cycles. Lithium nitride, $\ce{Li3N}$ is one of the well studied hydrogen storage material. Almost all absorbed hydrogen can be subsequently desorbed if the hydrogenated sample of $\ce{Li3N}$ is evacuated to 1 Pa and heated up to $450\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The hydrogen uptake of $\ce{Li3N}$ is a chemical reaction in two steps. Both steps involve disproportionation of $\ce{H2}$.

2.1 Complete the following equations by identifying $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

$$\ce{Li3N + H2 ->} \ \underset{\mathbf{A}}{\underline{\qquad\qquad}} + \underset{\mathbf{B}}{\underline{\qquad\qquad}}$$

$$(\mathbf{A}) + \ce{H2 ->} \ \underset{\mathbf{C}}{\underline{\qquad\qquad}} + \underset{\mathbf{B}}{\underline{\qquad\qquad}}$$

(1.5 marks)

2.2 Under standard conditions of temperature and pressure, calculate the maximum volume of hydrogen that can be stored in 1 kg of $\ce{Li3N}$. (1 mark)

When a certain mass of compound $\mathbf{B}$ was reacted with excess amount of $0.5\,\mathrm{M}$ HCl, a colourless gas was produced. Passing this gas over $\ce{CuO(s)}$ resulted in decrease in mass of the solid by 2.096 g.

2.3 (i) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with HCl
(ii) Calculate the mass of $\mathbf{B}$ taken in grams.

(1 mark)

Mg and $\ce{Mg2Ni}$ also form hydrides which can be desorbed under suitable conditions of temperature and pressure. $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ is formed by a technique known as hybriding combustion synthesis. $\ce{MgH2}$ is synthesised by the reaction of $\ce{H2}$ and Mg at high temperatures and pressure in presence of a catalyst.

2.4 In $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$, Ni(0) atoms form a face centered cubic lattice in which the $\ce{Mg^{+2}}$ ions occupy interstitial positions. The unit cell length of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ was found to be $6.465\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$.

A hydrogen cylinder at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ has number of moles of hydrogen per unit volume which is (1/100) times the number of moles of hydrogen present in unit volume of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$. Calculate the pressure (in bar) in this cylinder. (2 marks)

The desorption equilibrium of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ is as given below

$$\ce{Mg2NiH4(s) <=> Mg2Ni(s) + 2H2(g)}$$

The equilibrium pressure of hydrogen was found to be 7.03 bar and 1.05 bar at 606 K and 533 K respectively. Assume that the enthalpy values do not change with temperature and $\Delta H_f^\circ(\ce{Mg2NiH4}) = -176.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

2.5 Calculate the standard enthalpy change ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) for the reaction

$$\ce{2Mg(s) + Ni(s) <=> Mg2Ni(s)}$$

(1.5 marks)

B. Fuel cells – Green and renewable sources of energy

Fuel cells convert the chemical energy of combustion in a fuel directly into electrical energy without the losses associated with the use of thermodynamic heat engines. A group of researchers have invented a fuel cell using cane sugar ($\ce{C12H22O11}$). This system consists of two reaction vessels. The reaction vessel on the left hand side contains cane sugar and $\ce{VO^{2+}}$ ions in a strong acidic solution. Air is pumped in the right hand side vessel which also contains $\ce{VO^{2+}}$ ions in a strong acidic solution. The assembly contains a battery at the centre that is responsible to generate electricity.

In the left hand side vessel, $\ce{VO^{2+}}$ is reduced to $\ce{V^{3+}}$ and cane sugar is oxidised to $\ce{CO2}$. In the right hand side vessel, $\ce{VO^{2+}}$ is oxidised by oxygen to form $\ce{VO2+}$. The fuel cell diagram is indicated below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2014-2-fig1.png

(Ref: Excell Robert H.B and Spaziante Placido (2004), A fuel power cell powered by sugar, The Joint International Conference on “Sustainable Energy and Environment, Thailand, 1-3 Dec 2004.)

2.6 Write balanced equations for all the reactions in the (a) left side reaction vessel (b) right side reaction vessel. (2 marks)

2.7 Calculate the volume of air that has to be pumped in at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 101 kPa into the right side vessel, for the consumption of 10 g of cane sugar in the other vessel (air contains 21 % of volume oxygen). (1.5 marks)

2.8 Calculate the values of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ (in volts) from the given information.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2014-2-fig2.png

(1 mark)

In the battery at the centre between the reaction vessels, the following half cell reactions take place during discharge

$$\ce{V^{3+}(aq) + H2O <=> VO^{2+}(aq) + 2H+(aq) + e-} \quad \ldots\ldots\ \mathbf{I}$$

$$\ce{VO2+(aq) + 2H+(aq) + e- <=> VO^{2+}(aq) + H2O} \quad \ldots\ldots\ \mathbf{II}$$

The standard reduction potentials are $E^\circ(\ce{VO^{2+}}/\ce{V^{3+}}) = 0.34\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^\circ(\ce{VO2+}/\ce{VO^{2+}}) = 1.00\,\mathrm{V}$ respectively. Assume that the concentration of $\ce{V^{3+}(aq)}$ and $\ce{VO2+(aq)}$ is equal to $2.00\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ (obtained from the reactions taking place in the reaction vessels).

B. Volhard method is a back titration method and involves excess addition of $\ce{AgNO3}$ and its back titration with potassium thiocyanate using ferric alum as the indicator. The end point is the appearance of a reddish brown colour due to the formation of iron thiocyanate complex.

problems.title: Oxides of nitrogen
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 marks). Oxides of nitrogen

Nitrogen is one of the most important elements on earth. It forms several oxides including nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide. Nitric oxide is an air pollutant produced in the combustion processes in automobile engines and power plants.

1.1 Write the Lewis dot structures of nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide. (1 mark)

In the chemical industry, nitric oxide is an important intermediate produced by oxidation of ammonia by oxygen. This is the first step in the Ostwald’s process of the manufacture of nitric acid.

1.2 Write the balanced equation for the oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide by oxygen. (0.5 mark)

1.3 In a closed vessel, at 700 K and a pressure of 1 atm, 100 kmols of ammonia are mixed with 20% excess of air than that required for complete combustion of ammonia. (air contains 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen on volume basis)

i) Calculate the initial number of moles of oxygen and nitrogen present in the system. (1 mark)

ii) At equilibrium, 70% yield of nitric oxide was obtained in the closed vessel. Calculate the mole percent of ammonia and water present in the mixture at equilibrium. (2 marks)

Some equilibria of nitrogen oxides, which can be exploited commercially are shown below. (From Questions 1.4 to 1.8, you need to refer to these equations.)

$\mathbf{A}$) $\ce{N2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO(g)}$

$\mathbf{B}$) $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$

$\mathbf{C}$) $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$

$\mathbf{D}$) $\ce{2NO2(g) + H2O(aq) <=> HNO2(aq) + HNO3(aq)}$

1.4 Using the following data, calculate the standard free energy change in kJ for reaction $\mathbf{A}$. The temperature is 298.15 K.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Delta H_f^\circ \text{ of } \ce{NO(g)}:\ 90.37\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & S^\circ \text{ of } \ce{N2(g)}:\ 191.5\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ S^\circ \text{ of } \ce{O2(g)}:\ 205\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & S^\circ \text{ of } \ce{NO(g)}:\ 210.6\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \end{array}$$

(1.5 marks)

1.5 At 298.15 K, the $\Delta G^\circ$ of formation for $\ce{N2O4(g)}$, and $\ce{NO2(g)}$ are $98.28\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $51.84\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively. Starting with 1 mole of $\ce{N2O4(g)}$ at 1.0 atm and 298.15 K, calculate % of $\ce{N2O4}$ decomposed if the total pressure is kept constant at 1.0 atm and the temperature maintained at 298.15 K. (2 marks)

1.6 $\Delta H^\circ$ for the reaction $\mathbf{C}$ is 58.03 kJ. Assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ to be temperature independent, calculate the temperature at which the fraction of $\ce{N2O4}$ decomposed is double the value of that calculated in 1.5. (The pressure is 1 atm) (2.5 marks)

1.7 The equilibrium represented by $\mathbf{C}$ was studied at $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at a certain pressure. The density of the gaseous mixture was $5.85\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$. Calculate the average molecular weight of the gaseous mixture and the degree of dissociation of $\ce{N2O4}$ at $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. ($\Delta G^\circ = -1.254\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) (4 marks)

1.8 Nitric oxide is formed in the combustion of fuel. An internal combustion engine produces 250 ppm ($250\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$) of NO (w/v). 100 L of air containing the produced NO was oxidized to $\ce{NO2}$. The $\ce{NO2}$ formed was dissolved in 100 L of water. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. Refer to reaction $\mathbf{D}$. (Given: $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{HNO2} = 3.25$) (2.5 marks)

Two standard methods for estimation of amino acids are described below. In method I, a sample of valine is treated with nitrous acid and the volume of nitrogen gas released is measured. The reaction is as follows:

Problem 3 (26 marks). Organic Reaction Intermediates

Many organic reactions proceed through intermediates such as carbocations, carbanions, carbon radicals, carbenes etc. The structure and stability of the intermediates are the crucial factors that determine reaction mechanism. For example, in a reaction proceeding through formation of carbocation, the stability of the carbocation determines the rate of the reaction. Hammond postulate is an important tool to discuss transition state. It states that the transition state resembles that side closer to it in free energy.

problems.title: Beer-Lambert Law
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (12 marks). Beer-Lambert Law

A.

Beer–Lambert law deals with the relationship between the extent of absorption of radiation by a species and its concentration. The law states that ‘absorbance ($A$) is directly proportional to concentration (expressed as $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) at any given wavelength for a dilute solution. Mathematically it can be expressed as $A = \varepsilon\, l\, c$, where, $\varepsilon$ = molar absorptivity (units = $\mathrm{L\,cm^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$), $l$ = path length in cm, $A = -\log_{10}(I/I_\mathrm{o})$, where $I_\mathrm{o}$ = intensity of the incident radiation and $I$ = intensity of the transmitted radiation. The ratio of $(I/I_\mathrm{o})$ is called as transmittance ($T$).

Method of continuous variation is one of the standard methods used for the spectrophotometric determination of the composition of a complex between a metal $\mathbf{M}$ and a ligand $\mathbf{L}$. In this method, the sum of the molar concentrations of the metal $\mathbf{M}$ and the ligand $\mathbf{L}$ is kept constant, but their relative ratio is varied. The following graph is obtained for one such analysis. Use the graph to answer the questions from 6.1 to 6.4.

($X_\mathrm{M} = C_\mathrm{M}/(C_\mathrm{M} + C_\mathrm{L})$, where $C_\mathrm{M}$ = concentration of the metal ion in all forms, $C_\mathrm{L}$ = concentration of ligand in all forms).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2015-6-fig1.png

6.3 What percentage of the incident light is transmitted through solutions when (i) $X_\mathrm{M} = 0.1$ and when (ii) $X_\mathrm{L} = 0.2$? (1.5 marks)

problems.title: Sulphate dynamics in Wastewaters
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (20 marks). Sulphate dynamics in Wastewaters

Wastewaters are one of the highly complex chemical systems in our environment. Understanding these complex chemical reactions is important for safe management of wastewater systems. Here we look at some of the chemical dynamics of sulphate ions in wastewaters. Under scarcity of stronger oxidizers such as $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{NO3^-}$, $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ ions can act as oxidizing agents for organic matter in wastewater aiding its decomposition. Sulphate reduction is often facilitated by sulphate-reducing bacteria (SRB), which are usually present in sewage and thrive in an anaerobic (low oxygen) environment. Sulphate reduction can eventually lead to production of toxic $\ce{H2S}$ gas. The overall redox reaction can be represented by the equation:

$$\ce{SO4^{2-}(aq) + 9H3O+(aq) + 8e- <=> HS^-(aq) + 13H2O} \qquad E^\circ = -0.22\,\mathrm{V} \qquad (1)$$

$\ce{HS^-}$ thus produced gets converted into $\ce{H2S}$.

In sewage, organic matter is present predominantly as suspended solid particles, which can be represented as $\{\ce{CH2O}\}$. This matter can act as food for SRB and as a reducing agent for sulphate. The chemical transformation in the process can be represented as

$$\ce{SO4^{2-}(aq) + 2}\{\ce{CH2O}\}\ce{(s) + H3O+(aq) <=> HS^-(aq) + 2CO2(aq) + 3H2O(l)} \qquad E^\circ = 0.26\,\mathrm{V} \qquad (2)$$

For all parts in this problem, take temperature of the system to be $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

1.1 (1 mark) Determine the change in standard Gibbs free energy, $\Delta G^\circ$, for reaction (2) in kJ.

1.2 (1 mark) Write an expression for equilibrium constant, $K$, for reaction (2) in terms of molar concentrations of the relevant chemical species.

1.3 (1 mark) Calculate the value of $K$ for reaction (2).

1.4 (2 marks) A sewage entering a septic tank has $[\ce{SO4^{2-}}] = 0.5\,\mathrm{mM}$ and pH = 7.0. Assuming (2) to be the predominant redox reaction in the sewage, determine the concentration of dissolved $\ce{H2S}$ in it when the system reaches equilibrium. (For $\ce{H2S}$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a_1} = 7.0$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a_2} = 11.96$).

Assume that

(a) $\ce{H2S}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ gases produced remain in the solution phase.
(b) the carbonic acid produced here doesn't undergo dissociation.
(c) the sewage acts as buffer.

Under aerobic conditions, $\ce{CH4}$ is also often produced in the decomposition of sewage in addition to $\ce{H2S}$ and $\ce{CO2}$.

1.5 (2 marks) Following graphs show temperature dependence of solubilities of the three gases in water, which includes the gas in dissolved form as well as its reaction products with water.

i) Label the boxes in each graph with appropriate gas.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2016-1-fig1.png

ii) Which of the three gases will escape from sewage the fastest?

1.6 (2 marks) Septic tanks have a certain amount of air above the water level. In one such tank, the average composition of the air was found to be $\ce{N2}$ = 86%, $\ce{O2}$ = 9%, $\ce{H2O}$ = 1.5%, $\ce{CO2}$ = 1.5%, $\ce{H2S}$ = 1% and $\ce{CH4}$ = 1% (where the percentages are by mass). Calculate the average density of this air in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, assuming its pressure to be 1 atm and all gases to be ideal.

1.7 (1.5 marks) Unless there is turbulence or mixing, gases entering a chamber do not immediately diffuse uniformly in the chamber space. Initially they tend to accumulate in different horizontal zones according to their relative density compared to the air present in the chamber. Septic tanks are designed to have slow flow rate of sewage, therefore, do not have any significant turbulence in air inside. In the tank described in 1.6, indicate the zones in the air space (A, B, or C as shown below), in which each of the three gases ($\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{H2S}$, $\ce{CO2}$) escaping from the sewage would accumulate initially.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2016-1-fig2.png

[Answer boxes printed for: $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{H2S}$.]

1.8 (1.5 marks) Water vapour in this air condenses on the tank walls. $\ce{H2S}$ in the air then slowly dissolves in these droplets. Since oxygen is available in immediate vicinity of the droplets (because of high surface area to volume ratio as compared to sewage below), sulphur oxidizing bacteria (SOB) start accumulating in these droplets. In this new aqueous system, SOB oxidize sulphide species and produce sulphuric acid. The cement part in concrete walls can be represented as $\ce{(CaO)3(Al2O3)}$, which is attacked by sulphuric acid. Write the balanced reaction(s) responsible for sulphuric acid production in the water droplets and its possible reaction/s with the cement in concrete.

Wastewater from tanneries contains high amounts of $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ and Cr(VI) species. Since Cr(VI) species are highly toxic, such wastewater is often treated with reducing agents such as sucrose to reduce Cr(VI) to Cr(III) before discharging. However, on exposure to air, Cr(III) species may get oxidized back to $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$.

1.9 (4 marks) A tannery wastewater containing $50\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ Cr(III) and $100\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ having a pH = 7.0 is discharged in an open drain exposed to atmosphere. If atmospheric air contains 21.9% oxygen by mass, rest being predominantly nitrogen, calculate the ratio of $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ to Cr(III) after it has attained equilibrium with the atmospheric air.

$$\ce{O2(g) + 4H3O+(aq) + 4e- <=> 6H2O} \qquad E^\circ = 1.23\,\mathrm{V} \qquad (3)$$

$$\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}(aq) + 14H3O+(aq) + 6e- <=> 2Cr^{3+}(aq) + 21H2O} \qquad E^\circ = 1.36\,\mathrm{V} \qquad (4)$$

As wastewater flow in open drains, its volume slowly decreases due to evaporation of water. In the open drain described in 1.9, the water volume reduced by 30% on travelling 1 km.

1.10 (1.5 marks) Determine the equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$, Cr(III) and $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ in the wastewater after this 1 km travel.

After this 1 km stretch, the wastewater in 1.10 enters a closed sewer containing sewage, where oxygen is not available. Here, SRB would reduce sulphate to sulphide which can reduce $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ back to Cr(III).

1.11 (2.5 marks) Write balanced chemical equations for the reactions and their standard electrochemical potentials which would determine the concentrations of Cr(III) and $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ in this sewer, assuming they are solely driven by sulphate-sulphide inter-conversion.
