Problem 3 (17 marks). Chemical Kinetics and Nuclear Reactions

Part A

The reaction between $\ce{BrO3^-}$ and $\ce{Br^-}$ in acidic solution results in the formation of $\ce{Br2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ and the rate law is given by,

$$r = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{BrO3^-}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k\,[\ce{BrO3^-}]\,[\ce{Br^-}]\,[\ce{H^+}]^2$$

3.1 (1 mark) Write the stoichiometric equation corresponding to this reaction.

3.2 (1 mark) Write the total order of the reaction.

3.3 (1 mark) Simplify the rate law for the same reaction if $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0 = 2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$, $[\ce{H^+}]_0 = 1.0\,\mathrm{M}$ and $[\ce{Br^-}]_0 = 0.28\,\mathrm{M}$ where the subscript zero refers to initial concentration.

To study the kinetics of the above reaction, a student added phenol to the above reaction mixture, which undergoes the following reaction:

$$\ce{Br2 + C6H5OH -> BrC6H4OH + Br^-}$$

To detect the completion of the above monobromination reaction, the student added a drop of dilute methyl orange solution to the reaction flask. Methyl orange gets bleached by $\ce{Br2}$ and becomes colourless immediately even at very low $\ce{Br2}$ concentrations.

Monobromination of phenol, ($\ce{C6H5OH}$) is a much faster reaction than the bromate-bromide reaction. The student prepared three reaction flasks as given in the table below. The student measured the time, $t$, it takes for the solution at different concentrations of phenol to turn colourless.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Flask No.} & [\ce{C6H5OH}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & [\ce{Br^-}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & [\ce{H^+}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & [\ce{BrO3^-}]^{*}\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Time taken for decolourization, } t\ (\mathrm{sec}) \\ \hline 1 & 4\times10^{-3} & 0.28 & 1.0 & 2.5\times10^{-3} & 11 \\ 2 & 2\times10^{-3} & 0.28 & 1.0 & 2.5\times10^{-3} & 4 \\ 3 & 1\times10^{-3} & 0.28 & 1.0 & 2.5\times10^{-3} & 1.5 \end{array}$$

$^{*}\ce{BrO3^-}$ is added in the last just before starting the experimental run.

3.4 (2 marks) On doubling the concentration of $\ce{C6H5OH}$, (in the above table) $t$ increased by more than a factor of two because (put X against the correct option/s)

i) the decolouration reaction of methyl orange slowed down at higher concentration of phenol
ii) the bromination of phenol slowed down at higher concentration of phenol
iii) at higher concentration of phenol, $\ce{BrC6H4OH}$ started converting to $\ce{Br2C6H3OH}$
iv) the rate of bromate-bromide reaction decreases with progress of reaction overtime.
v) at higher concentration of phenol, the simplified rate law derived in 3.3 is no longer valid

3.5 (3 marks) Calculate the rate constant, $k$, of bromate-bromide reaction using the data given in the above table. Show all important steps in the calculations.

3.6 (2 marks) Another way to do this experiment is to keep the phenol concentration fixed and vary $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0$. In such an experiment, (mark X against the correct option/s)

(i) $t$ will increase as $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0$ increases
(ii) $k$ can be obtained from the initial slope of $[\ce{BrO3^-}]$ vs $t$ plot fit to an exponential curve
(iii) the experiment become less accurate as $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0/[\ce{C6H5OH}]_0$ decreases
(iv) $t$ will be independent of $[\ce{Br^-}]_0$
(v) $k$ can be obtained using the slope of $1/t$ vs $[\ce{BrO3^-}]$ plot fit to a line

Part B

Green nickel oxide NiO can be doped with colorless lithium oxide, $\ce{Li2O}$, to give a black solid $\ce{Li_{x}Ni_{1-x}O}$ which acts as a semiconductor.

5.6 (1 mark) Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct for the above observations? (Mark X in the correct box)

i) $\ce{Li_{x}Ni_{1-x}O}$ exhibits both cationic and anionic vacancies
ii) $\ce{Li_{x}Ni_{1-x}O}$ exhibits Schottky defect
iii) Doping of NiO with lithium induces mixed valency of nickel
iv) NiO becomes a p-type semiconductor

Mixed metal oxides of transition metals often form spinels having the general formula $\mathrm{A^{II}B^{III}_2O_4}$ where the oxide ions form a close packed cubic lattice with eight tetrahedral holes and four octahedral holes per $\mathrm{A^{II}B^{III}_2O_4}$ unit. In a normal spinel 1/8th of the tetrahedral holes are occupied by A (II) whereas B (III) resides in octahedral sites. In inverse spinel A (II) and one half of B (III) occupy the octahedral holes while the other half of B (III) occupy the tetrahedral holes. The structure becomes 'normal' ($\mathrm{A^{II}B^{III}_2O_4}$) or 'inverse' spinel ($\mathrm{B^{III}A^{II}B^{III}O_4}$) depending upon the octahedral site preference energy which is the difference of the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) of the same cation in the corresponding octahedral and tetrahedral field of the ligand.

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} \text{Metal ion} & \Delta_0\ (\mathrm{cm^{-1}}) & \Delta_t\ (\mathrm{cm^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{Co^{3+}} & 20{,}760 & 9{,}226 \\ \ce{Fe^{3+}} & 14{,}000 & 6{,}220 \\ \ce{Ni^{2+}} & 8{,}500 & 3{,}780 \end{array}$$

($\Delta_0$ and $\Delta_t$ imply the octahedral and tetrahedral splitting parameters respectively for oxide ions which will provide a moderately weak field similar to that of water)

5.7 (2.5 marks) On the basis of the above data, calculate the CFSE for

Case I: i) Co(III) in octahedral ii) Co(III) in tetrahedral sites

Case II: i) Fe (III) in octahedral ii) Fe(III) in tetrahedral sites

Case III: i) Ni(II) in octahedral ii) Ni(II) in tetrahedral sites

(Calculations involving pairing energies can be neglected for this question and only CFSE values can be calculated)

iii) (1 mark) Calculate the octahedral site preference energy from 5.7 for all the above three cases.

iv) (1 mark) Based on the above octahedral site preference energy calculations, classify the oxides as normal and inverse spinels. (Mark X in the correct box)

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \text{Normal} & \text{Inverse} \\ \hline \ce{NiFe2O4} & \square & \square \\ \ce{NiCo2O4} & \square & \square \end{array}$$

5.8 One of the widely used batteries of nickel is Ni-Cd battery. This battery uses high purity NiOOH (nickel oxyhydroxide) as anode. The typical synthesis of NiOOH is as follows.

In the first step, concentrated NaOH (30% w/v) is reacted with gaseous $\ce{Cl2}$ for sufficient time to generate hypochlorite.

i) (0.5 mark) Write balanced chemical equation for this reaction.

The resultant reaction mixture is then treated with excess of solid NaOH with vigorous stirring which leads to precipitation of NaCl. The precipitate is filtered and the sufficient amount of $\ce{Ni(OH)2}$ is added to the filtrate with constant stirring. Black colored NiOOH is formed as suspension.

ii) (1 mark) Write the balanced chemical equation that leads to formation of NiOOH.

The NiOOH suspension thus obtained is filtered and dried appropriately. However, before its use, it needs to be analyzed for its purity.

In one such analysis, $0.520\,\mathrm{g}$ of NiOOH sample prepared by the above method was treated with $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ of acidified $0.305\,\mathrm{M}$ Fe (II) solution. On dissolution, Fe(II) ions get oxidized quantitatively by Ni ions. The unreacted Fe(II) was titrated with $0.0285\,\mathrm{M}$ of $\ce{KMnO4}$ under acidic condition and the observed reading was $15.1\,\mathrm{mL}$.

5.9 (1 mark) Write balanced chemical equations for-

i) Reaction of NiOOH with acidified Fe(II)
ii) Reaction involved in titration with $\ce{KMnO4}$

iii) (2 marks) Calculate the percentage of NiOOH in the sample taken for analysis. Show the main steps of calculations.

problems.title: Barbiturates in our lives
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 marks). Barbiturates in our lives

Guano, the excreta of sea birds and bats was a major export item from colonial America to Europe in the 19th century used for making fertilizers and extracting uric acid, which was used to produce many commercial chemicals including the valuable dye Murexide. Uric acid is a metabolic by-product of proteins and nucleic acids. German chemist Adolf von Baeyer in 1864, while studying the chemistry of uric acid, discovered barbituric acid $\mathbf{C}$. Derivatives of this compound were very effective in inducing sleep in animals. Later, this family of compounds turned out to be very effective drugs for human psychological disorders.

In a few years, a simple procedure to produce $\mathbf{C}$ was found using $\ce{POCl3}$ mediated condensation of compound $\mathbf{A}$ ($\ce{C3H4O4}$) derived from apple juice and compound $\mathbf{B}$ ($\ce{CH4N2O}$), abundant in animal excreta.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-1-fig1.png

$\mathbf{C}$

1.1 Draw structures for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Thiopental, popularly known as "truth serum", which makes people to speak more (often revealing the truth) was soon discovered. It has a ring structure similar to $\mathbf{C}$. Its preparation involves reacting 2-ethyl-propanedioic acid diethyl ester with racemic 2-bromopentane in the presence of sodium ethoxide to form product $\mathbf{D}$ ($\ce{C14H26O4}$). $\mathbf{D}$ obtained, is a racemic mixture, which condenses with thiourea to give Thiopental ($\mathbf{E}$) ($\ce{C11H18N2O2S}$). The 'R' isomer of Thiopental is a mood elevator and the 'S' isomer causes neurological depression.

1.2 Draw the structure of $\mathbf{D}$ and the two isomers of $\mathbf{E}$ and label them with 'R' and 'S' configuration.

1.3 Compound $\mathbf{C}$ is quite acidic ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 4.01$). Draw the structures of the most stable tautomers of the conjugate base of $\mathbf{C}$. The tautomers should be unique and not resonance structures of each other.

Compound $\mathbf{F}$ ($\ce{C4H2N2O4}$) is one of the oldest synthesised organic compounds, discovered by Justus von Liebig and Friedrich Wöhler in 1938. It was used to produce the dye murexide. When ingested, it accumulates in the pancreas damaging insulin-producing cells and causing Type II diabetes mellitus. Due to this, it is used to induce diabetes in laboratory rats in diabetes research.

1.4 $\mathbf{F}$ is formed in the $\ce{CrO3}$ oxidation of the condensation product $\mathbf{G}$ of benzaldehyde and $\mathbf{C}$ in the presence of piperidine (a base). Draw the structures of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-1-fig2.png

1.5 The condensation reaction above giving $\mathbf{G}$ proceeds well. This shows that the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of the conjugate acid of piperidine is (mark X in the correct box)
a) $< 4.01$
b) $> 4.01$
c) $= 4.01$

In neutral aqueous solution, $\mathbf{F}$ exists as a ketal $\mathbf{H}$. At acidic pH, $\mathbf{H}$ reverts to $\mathbf{F}$. When reduced with hydrogen sulphide, $\mathbf{F}$ gave $\mathbf{I}$, which in the presence of excess $\mathbf{F}$ gives hemiketal $\mathbf{J}$. Compound $\mathbf{J}$ on treatment with $\ce{NH3}$ gives the dye murexide.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-1-fig3.png

1.6 Identify the structures $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{J}$.

In 1933, Paul György and Richard Kuhn isolated a yellow pigment which turned out to be an essential vitamin and a cure for many diseases. Later, it was identified as Compound $\mathbf{K}$ ($\ce{C17H20N4O6}$) with a D-aldopentose ($\mathbf{L}$) derived side chain. In $\mathbf{L}$, C3 carbon has 'R' configuration.

1.7 $\mathbf{L}$ ($\ce{C5H10O5}$) on reduction with sodium borohydride ($\ce{NaBH4}$) gives an optically inactive alditol. Draw the Fischer projection formula of $\mathbf{L}$ with correct configuration at all chiral carbons.

1.8 One of the chemical syntheses of $\mathbf{K}$ involves a series of reactions as given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-1-fig4.png

a) Identify structures $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{N}$, and $\mathbf{O}$.

b) $\mathbf{K}$ ($\ce{C17H20N4O6}$), obtained by condensation of $\mathbf{O}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ has a ring structure. The template of the structure of $\mathbf{K}$ is shown below. Using the given template, complete the structure of $\mathbf{K}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-1-fig5.png

1.9 Degradation studies of $\mathbf{K}$ had played an important role in its identification. Alkaline hydrolysis of $\mathbf{K}$ with $1\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gave $\mathbf{P}$ ($\ce{C16H19N2NaO7}$) by losing a mole of $\mathbf{B}$. Further hydrolysis of $\mathbf{P}$ by $5\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gave $\mathbf{Q}$ ($\ce{C13H22N2O4}$). Draw structure of $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.

problems.title: Chemistry of Iron
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (26 marks). Chemistry of Iron

Part A: Iron Sulphur proteins

Iron is the most prevalent transition metal in living systems. Let us look at proteins containing iron that play an important role in electron transfer (i.e., oxidation–reduction) reactions in living systems.

Fe–S protein(s) is an important class of proteins, containing iron and sulphur in their core. These proteins have been discovered in last mid-century and seem to be highly abundant in living systems. Their core Fe-S clusters can be synthesized in laboratory in absence of oxygen. Their properties make one to believe that they could have been the biomolecules shaping the origins of life on earth when anaerobic conditions were most prevalent.

The simplest Fe-S unit is found in rubredoxin protein that contains one iron and four cysteine amino acid [$\ce{HOOCCH(NH2)CH2SH}$] units. In 1981, Hagen and co-workers in USA synthesized an analogue of rubredoxin, $\ce{(Et4N)2[Fe(SPh)4]}$, where Et = $\ce{-C2H5}$, Ph = $\ce{-C6H5}$. (In the following questions, consider sulphur as a weak field ligand.)

2.1 Predict the geometry of $\ce{[Fe(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ and draw its appropriate structure. Calculate its magnetic moment.

The next simplest Fe-S units found in proteins are 2Fe-2S, 4Fe-4S and 3Fe-4S. These units have two types of Fe-S bonds and no Fe-Fe bonds.

a) 2Fe-2S – This unit has two sulphide ions ($\ce{S^{2-}}$) and four cysteine residues bonded to two iron centers. Hagen and co-workers synthesized an analogue of this cluster, $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ from $\ce{[Fe(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ and elemental sulphur.

2.2 Complete and balance the chemical equation given below.

$$\ce{[Fe(SPh)4]^{2-}} + \ce{S} \longrightarrow \ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}} + \ce{PhSSPh} + \underset{(\mathrm{X})}{\underline{\qquad}}$$

2.3 Draw the structure of $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ unit.

b) 4Fe-4S – This unit has four sulphide ions and four cysteine residues bonded to four iron centers. The analogue, $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ was spontaneously obtained from $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ using suitable reaction medium.

2.4 Give the balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ from $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$.

$$\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}} \longrightarrow \ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}} + \underset{(\mathrm{Y})}{\underline{\qquad}} + \underset{(\mathrm{Z})}{\underline{\qquad}}$$

2.5 Draw the structure of $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ that has a cubic core.

2.6 The number of Fe (III) and Fe (II) ions in $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ and $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ are– (Indicate the numbers in the boxes):
a) Fe (III) in $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$
b) Fe (II) in $\ce{[Fe2S2(SPh)4]^{2-}}$
c) Fe (III) in $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$
d) Fe (II) in $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$

2.7 Using the above cubic structure of $\ce{[Fe4S4(SPh)4]^{2-}}$ as reference, draw the structure of $\ce{[Fe3S4(SPh)3]^{2-}}$, another analogue unit of iron-sulphur proteins, labeled as 3Fe-4S.

2.8 At pH > 9 and with availability of excess thiophenol, $\ce{[Fe3S4(SPh)3]^{2-}}$ gets converted to a linear structure with a molecular formula of $\ce{[Fe3S4(SPh)4]^{3-}}$. Draw the structure of $\ce{[Fe3S4(SPh)4]^{3-}}$.

2.9 Following are different types of Fe-S bonds in the above clusters. Mark X for— the most ionic Fe-S bond / the least ionic Fe-S bond
a) $\ce{C6H5S-Fe}$(III)
b) $\ce{C6H5S-Fe}$(II)
c) S-Fe(III)
d) S-Fe(II)

[In the printed table each bond has one box in the column "the most ionic Fe-S bond" and one box in the column "the least ionic Fe-S bond".]

Generally, Fe compounds have very high magnetic moments due to which they are often used in magnetic applications. Some of the Fe-S units, however, exhibit low or no magnetic moments. This observation is attributed to opposite spin orientations of electrons in neighbouring metal centres within the same unit — a property also known as antiferromagnetic coupling.

2.10 In which of the following units (R = cysteine group), it is possible to have zero net magnetic moment due to antiferromagnetic coupling? (Mark X in the correct box (es))
a) $\ce{[Fe2S2(SR)4]^{3-}}$
b) $\ce{[Fe2S2(SR)4]^{2-}}$
c) $\ce{[Fe4S4(SR)4]^{2-}}$

Redox potential of $\ce{[Fe2S2(SR)4]^{3-}}$/$\ce{[Fe2S2(SR)4]^{2-}}$ couple (R = cysteine group) changes as the charges on the peptide chain in the extended part of the protein change through protonation/deprotonation of various groups such as amide –NH– groups. The following simplified schematic figures indicate two possible charge distribution on the peptide chain around $\ce{[Fe2S2(SR)4]^{3-}}$.

2.11 In which of these two systems, the iron centres are less prone to oxidation? (Mark X in correct box)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-2-fig1.png

In respiration cycle, $\ce{O2}$ gets converted to $\ce{H2O}$. In this process, superoxide, $\ce{O2^-}$ is generated, which is believed to be responsible for the process of ageing by damaging cell membranes. Body cells have an enzyme called superoxide dismutase (SOD), which converts $\ce{O2^-}$ into $\ce{O2}$ by abstracting an electron. SOD has two 3d transition metal ions ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) in +2 oxidation state. Some features of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are –

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \hline \text{Colour in +2 state in octahedral coordination} & \text{Yes} & \text{No} \\ \hline \text{Other possible oxidation states} & +1 & \text{No} \end{array}$$

2.12 $\mathbf{A}$ is ____ ; $\mathbf{B}$ is ____

2.13 The ion that can convert $\ce{O2^-}$ into $\ce{O2}$ is (Mark X in correct box)
• $\mathbf{A}^{2+}$
• $\mathbf{B}^{2+}$

Part B: Use of iron in "blue" colours

British astronomer and photographer John Hershel used Fe-based reagents to obtain a blue pigment (known as Turnbull's Blue) to develop the blue printing technique in 1842. Now, blue printing can be easily carried out using photochemical redox chemistry of potassium ferrioxalate.

Potassium ferrioxalate is synthesized by adding aqueous ferric nitrate to hot aqueous potassium oxalate. To optimize this process, it is important to determine the molar ratio of iron and oxalate in the complex that can be done using redox titrations. In one such analysis, $0.250\,\mathrm{g}$ of potassium ferrioxalate sample was taken to a flask and $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $4\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ was added to it. After making the solution hot, it was titrated with $0.0196\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KMnO4}$ till light pink colour was obtained. The observed burette reading was $31.1\,\mathrm{mL}$ which indicates oxalate content present in the complex.

2.14 Write the balanced half-cell equations for the reaction involved in the titration of oxalate with $\ce{KMnO4}$.

After this titration, excess of zinc powder was added to the same flask that led to effervescence in the solution. When the effervescence subsided, the solution was boiled for 10-15 minutes. The flask was cooled to room temperature and was titrated with the same $\ce{KMnO4}$ solution. (The solution was still acidic). The observed burette reading was $5.1\,\mathrm{mL}$. This will give the iron content in the sample.

2.15 Write the possible balanced chemical equation (s) for reaction (s) taking place after Zn dust is added to the flask.

2.16 Write the balanced half cell equations for the reaction involved in the titration of iron with $\ce{KMnO4}$.

2.17 Calculate the moles of iron and oxalate present in the sample and their molar ratio. (Show the main steps in your calculation).
• Calculations for oxalate content
• Calculations for iron content
• Molar ratio of iron : oxalate (to the nearest whole number)

2.18 a) Based on the above calculations draw the structure of the ferrioxalate complex ion formed. Represent the oxalate ligand as

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-2-fig2.png

b) How many isomers are possible for this complex? (Mark X in correct box (es))
i) two cis, one trans and trans giving two optical isomers
ii) only two optical isomers
iii) two cis, one trans and each of the cis forming two optical isomers each
iv) one cis, one trans and trans giving two optical isomers

2.19 In blue printing, a ferrioxalate salt is coated on a surface. Light is shone on this surface through a template of design that is to be printed. On regions of surface exposed to light, ferrioxalate ion undergoes photochemical reduction with the evolution of a gas which is acidic in aqueous solution.

a) Write the balanced chemical equation for this photochemical reaction.

This surface when dipped in potassium ferricyanide solution produces a blue coloured ferroferricyanide complex.

b) Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction.

problems.title: Understanding Milk
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (26 marks). Understanding Milk

Milk is regarded as a complete food for infants of mammals as it contains all the nutrients like carbohydrates, proteins, fats, minerals and vitamins required by them.

Part A: Proteins in Milk

Milk proteins are categorized into two groups:
(i) the water soluble whey proteins and
(ii) the caseins that have low aqueous solubility and exist in milk as micelles.

Adding a mild acid or alcohol leads to precipitation of casein, while whey proteins remain soluble. Caseins act as carriers of (otherwise insoluble) calcium phosphate through amino acids serine and threonine (in its peptide chains), whose side groups form ester linkages with the phosphate units of calcium phosphate.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig1.png

Phospho-ester groups in proteins typically have a $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1}$ of about 2.0 and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2}$ of about 7.0. The isoelectric point (the pH at which net charge on the species is zero) of caseins is at pH 4.6. A generalized polypeptide sequence can be represented as

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig2.png

where '$\mathrm{R_n}$' represents side chains present in amino acids.

4.1 If the amino acid bearing $\mathrm{R_n}$ in a casein protein is threonine, draw the structure of $\mathrm{R_n}$ in the templates given below (assuming that ester linkages are not broken due to hydrolysis).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig3.png

Casein proteins have hydrophobic as well as polar parts. Clustering of these proteins form micellar structures which, in fresh milk, have a net negative charge. Repulsion between these micelles stabilizes them in aqueous phase. Fresh milk has a pH of ~ 6.4 - 6.8. With time, milk tends to turn sour. Acidification tends to break phosphoester linkages. Baking soda ($\ce{NaHCO3}$) is sometimes added to souring milk to increase its shelf life.

4.2 Identify the correct statements from the following (Mark X in the appropriate box):
(a) Caseins would coagulate at pH < 6.4.
(b) Caseins would coagulate at pH < 4.6.
(c) Caseins would coagulate only at pH ~ <2.0.
(d) At pH < 4.6, $\ce{Ca3(PO4)2}$ would precipitate out.
(e) At pH < 2.0, both $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ would tend to dissociate from casein micelles and dissolve in the aqueous phase.
(f) Adding baking soda prevents coagulation of casein by consuming $\ce{H+}$.

Protein content of a milk sample is usually estimated by two methods:

(i) Kjeldahl method (estimation of total N in sample): This is the commonly used method by food inspection agencies. Milk sample is heated with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ with a catalyst, when all N is converted to ammonium ions. Then, this solution is made alkaline and ammonia is distilled into an excess of boric acid ($\ce{H3BO3}$) solution. The resultant solution is then titrated with a standard acid using a suitable indicator. From the amount of ammonia liberated, the N content is determined.

4.3 In the Kjeldahl's method, write balanced equations of the reaction of ammonia and boric acid, and that involved in the titration with HCl.

(ii) Biuret test (estimation of the amount of proteins): The sample is mixed with an excess of Biuret reagent ($\ce{CuSO4}$ in an alkaline solution). The amide units in proteins coordinate with $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions to form a violet coloured complex, which absorbs light of wavelength $540\,\mathrm{nm}$. This phenomenon of absorption is used to estimate the amount of complex formed which indicates the amount of protein. Aqueous $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ does not absorb at this wavelength.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig4.png

4.4 In Biuret test, addition of excess reagent is needed to ensure that (Mark X in the correct box):
a) all amide N in protein complex with $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$.
b) all $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions in the mixture are bound to proteins.
c) the violet colour developed is intense (to be detectable).

Milk suppliers often dilute milk with water to make profit. This reduces the protein content of the milk and can be easily caught by the Kjeldahl test. To get the diluted milk samples pass the Kjeldahl test, these suppliers add water soluble N-rich compounds as adulterants.

A food analysis lab received a milk sample $\mathbf{M}$ that was suspected to be adulterated.

4.5 A $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ portion of $\mathbf{M}$ was subjected to Kjeldahl analysis. When the ammonia collected into boric acid (aq.) was titrated with HCl solution ($0.140\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$), $35.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of HCl was consumed. Calculate the protein content (in $\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$) that would be reported for this sample based on this analysis. (In general, milk proteins contain 15.65% N.)

4.6 To another $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ portion of $\mathbf{M}$, sufficient amount of acetic acid was added to ensure coagulation of casein. After filtering off the solid part, the filtrate was subjected to Kjeldahl analysis as above. In the titration, $7.6\,\mathrm{mL}$ of HCl solution ($0.140\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) was consumed. Calculate the casein content (in $\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$) in the milk sample.

The sample was further taken for Biuret analysis.

4.7 A series of standard solutions of milk proteins of known concentrations 0.1, 0.5, 1.2 and $2.4\,\mathrm{mg\,mL^{-1}}$ were prepared. To $2\,\mathrm{mL}$ of each of the above solutions, excess Biuret reagent (constant amount for each solution) was added. After 30 min, the absorbance values of these mixtures was measured at $540\,\mathrm{nm}$, which is proportional to concentration of the light-absorbing species. Following plot shows the absorbance values for the protein concentration of solutions taken.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig5.png

To another $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of milk sample $\mathbf{M}$, sufficient amount of acetic acid was added to coagulate casein. This mixture was filtered and $8\,\mathrm{mL}$ filtrate was obtained. $2\,\mathrm{mL}$ of this filtrate on reaction with the same amount of Biuret reagent (as added to standard solutions above) gave an absorbance value of 0.66 at $540\,\mathrm{nm}$.

Using this data, calculate the concentration of non-protein N (if present) in $\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$ in the milk sample.

The remaining filtrate in part 4.7 was subjected to the following qualitative tests to check presence of any adulterant.
• a. On heating with concentrated NaOH evolved a gas which turned moist turmeric paper deep red.
• b. Addition of barium nitrate solution gave a white precipitate which was insoluble in dilute nitric acid.

4.8 Identify the possible adulterant(s) in the milk sample $\mathbf{M}$ based on above observations. (Mark X in the appropriate box):
a) Urea
b) $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$
c) $\ce{NaHCO3}$
d) $\ce{NaNO3}$

Part B: Carbohydrates in Milk

Lactose is the major carbohydrate present in milk, which is produced in mammary glands by α-lacto albumin— a major component of whey proteins. Natural milk does not contain sucrose, starch, maltose, etc found in plant sources. Lactose is a disaccharide formed from D(+) galactose and D(+)glucose. The Haworth formulae for α anomers of glucose and galactose are given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig6.png

On reaction with concentrated $\ce{HNO3}$, galactose ($\mathbf{P}$) gives compound $\mathbf{Q}$ ($\ce{C6H10O8}$).

4.9 Draw Fisher projection of $\mathbf{Q}$ and determine if it would be optically active or inactive. (Mark X in the appropriate box)
• Optically active
• Optically inactive

4.10 Draw the Haworth formula of the anomer of galactose $\mathbf{P}$.

Usually, 6-membered rings are more stable in chair conformations. Substitutents on ring, such as methyl group in methyl cyclohexane shown here, are more stable in equatorial position.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig7.png

Generally, in case of multiple substituents, a conformation with more substituents in equatorial positions is more stable.

4.11 Lactose has two anomeric structures $\mathbf{L_1}$ and $\mathbf{L_2}$. Haworth formula for $\mathbf{L_1}$ is given below. Complete the partial structure of the stable conformation of $\mathbf{L_1}$ with the two rings in chair forms (template for one of the rings is given).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig8.png

[Template printed in the answer box:]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-4-fig9.png

Lactose $\mathbf{L_1}$ reacts with $\ce{NH2OH}$ to give compound $\mathbf{R}$ ($\ce{C12H23NO11}$).

4.12 Draw the Haworth formula of $\mathbf{R}$.

Lactose forms $\mathbf{L_1}$ and $\mathbf{L_2}$ have specific optical rotations, +89.4° and +35°, respectively at 20 °C, while lactose solution at equilibrium (having these two forms) has specific optical rotation +55.7°.

4.13 From this data, determine the percentages of $\mathbf{L_1}$ and $\mathbf{L_2}$ in a lactose solution at equilibrium.

4.14 $\mathbf{L_1}$ and $\mathbf{L_2}$ have solubilities of $70\,\mathrm{g}$ and $500\,\mathrm{g}$, respectively in $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water at 20 °C. A student dissolved $400\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{L_2}$ crystals in $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water and kept this solution in a closed bottle at 20 °C. The next day she found white crystals growing in the bottle indicating some lactose has solidified out of the solution. Determine the total amount of lactose in the solution at this stage.

In recent decades, synthetic milk is being prepared by mixing cheap proteins, oils and surfactants with carbohydrates such as sucrose or starch. Two samples of milk, $\mathbf{Y_1}$ and $\mathbf{Y_2}$, were received in a laboratory, which were suspected of adulteration with synthetic milk.

These samples were taken through a process in which carbohydrates can be selectively extracted. From $\mathbf{Y_1}$ and $\mathbf{Y_2}$, respectively, carbohydrates were obtained as white crystalline solids $\mathbf{Y_{1S}}$ and $\mathbf{Y_{2S}}$, both of which were completely soluble in water. Solutions of both $\mathbf{Y_{1S}}$ and $\mathbf{Y_{2S}}$ had +ve optical rotations, but after adding small amount of HCl (aq) to both, $\mathbf{Y_{1S}}$ solution had –ve optical rotation while $\mathbf{Y_{2S}}$ solution had still +ve optical rotation. The analyst knew that sucrose is made of D (+) glucose and D(−) fructose, while starch is a polymer of D (+) glucose.

4.15 Based on this data, the analyst can conclude that (For each statement, mark X in correct box: Yes / No).
a) $\mathbf{Y_1}$ had synthetic milk added to it.
b) No synthetic milk was present in $\mathbf{Y_2}$.
c) $\mathbf{Y_1}$ had no lactose in it.
d) $\mathbf{Y_1}$ had sucrose in it.
e) No starch was present in $\mathbf{Y_1}$.
f) $\mathbf{Y_2}$ had starch in it.

problems.title: Isotope Effects
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (21 marks). Isotope Effects

In the last century, the discovery of deuterium has contributed most remarkably to our understanding of isotopes and expanded the limits of isotope applications. Deuterated compounds serve as non-radioactive isotopic tracers to study chemical reactions, particularly in biological systems, as deuterium substitution can change the physico-chemical properties of compounds.

The discovery of deuterium in 1931 is credited to American chemist Harold Urey, who observed the atomic spectrum of deuterium as faint lines accompanying the Balmer series lines of atomic hydrogen.

5.1 For a H atom with a nucleus of mass $M$ and an electron of mass $m$, the wavelength of light emitted corresponding to Balmer series is inversely proportional to the 'reduced mass' $\mu$ of the atom, defined as:

$$\mu = \frac{mM}{(m+M)}$$

If the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series for hydrogen ($\lambda_\mathrm{H}$) is 6564.74 Å, what would be the difference in wavelengths of the first lines in Balmer series for deuterium and hydrogen (i.e., $\lambda_\mathrm{H} - \lambda_\mathrm{D}$) as observed by Urey? (Note that $M_\mathrm{H} = 1.6737\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $M_\mathrm{D} = 3.3436\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$)

The lines observed by Urey for D spectrum were faint because of the low amounts of D naturally present in hydrogen gas samples (average 0.1998 mol% HD and negligible $\ce{D2}$). To establish that the faint lines were not the result of impurities, Urey tried to increase the proportion of D in the hydrogen gas samples – a process known as 'isotopic enrichment'.

This was achieved by slow evaporation, which exploited the difference in the vapour pressure of liquid $\ce{H2}$ and HD. At $14.1\,\mathrm{K}$ and $53\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$, Urey theoretically estimated the ratio of vapour pressures of pure liquids $p^\circ_\mathrm{HD}/p^\circ_\mathrm{H_2} = 0.4$ (use this information for question below).

Consider $2.002\,\mathrm{g}$ of liquid hydrogen (0.20 mol% HD; density = $0.077\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$) introduced in an evacuated sealed $12\,\mathrm{L}$ flask at $14\,\mathrm{K}$. It is allowed to slowly evaporate and attain equilibrium when the pressure measured was $53\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$.

5.2 Determine the moles of gas molecules present in the flask at equilibrium. Assume that both $\ce{H2}$ and HD show ideal gas behavior. Note that volume changes in liquid hydrogen during evaporation are negligible compared to the gaseous volume. (For all calculations in this part, take numbers upto 4th decimal)

5.3 What would be the mol% of HD in the liquid phase at equilibrium?

5.4 Efficiency of an enrichment process is gauged by the separation factor ($\alpha$), defined as

$$\alpha = \frac{x'_\mathrm{HD}/x'_\mathrm{H2}}{x_\mathrm{HD}/x_\mathrm{H2}}$$

(where, $x_\mathrm{HD}$ and $x'_\mathrm{HD}$ represents the mole fraction of HD in the sample before and after processing, respectively. Similarly, $x_\mathrm{H2}$ and $x'_\mathrm{H2}$ represents the corresponding mole fractions of $\ce{H2}$). For the evaporation process described above, what is the enrichment factor of HD in the residual liquid?

5.5 Density of a gas often reflects its isotopic composition. Consider a gas sample containing $\ce{H2}$ and HD mixed in a $1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ container. The gas weighs $0.1105\,\mathrm{g}$ at standard temperature and pressure. Determine the mol percentage of HD in the sample. (Assume ideal gas behavior for both HD and $\ce{H2}$).

Deuterium enrichment in liquid water can also be achieved by prolonged electrolysis of water, using the small difference in electrode potentials for reduction of $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{D+}$. For the electrode reaction:

$$\ce{H+(aq) + D+(aq) + 2e- <=> HD(g)}, \qquad E^0 = -0.0076\,\mathrm{V} \text{ with reference to Standard Hydrogen Electrode}$$

5.6 For the following statements, mark X in the appropriate box (True / False).
a) HD has a lower tendency to get oxidized as compared to $\ce{H2}$.
b) Deuterium enrichment will occur in the aqueous phase.
c) $\ce{H+}$ has a greater tendency to get reduced as compared to $\ce{D+}$.
d) HD will not form at cathode.

5.7 Write the half-cell reaction possible at the anode with HDO as reacting species.

5.8 In the following cell meant for electrolysis of water, if the solution is not stirred, in which part of cell ($\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{B}$) one can expect a higher concentration of HDO once electrolysis has started? (Mark X in the appropriate box)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-5-fig1.png

(i) $\mathbf{A}$
(ii) $\mathbf{B}$
(iii) equal in $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$

Water chemistry becomes more interesting and challenging when isotopes are considered. For example, artificial mixtures of 'light' water ($\ce{H2O}$) and heavy water ($\ce{D2O}$) undergo self-dissociation and recombination process to yield a mixture of $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{D2O}$ and HDO. The equilibrium can be represented as:

$$\ce{H2O(l) + D2O(l) <=> 2HDO(l)} \qquad (K_\mathrm{eq} = 3.86 \text{ at } 298\,\mathrm{K})$$

Note that here $K_\mathrm{eq} = [\mathrm{HDO}\,(l)]\,/\,[\mathrm{H_2O}\,(l)][\mathrm{D_2O}\,(l)]$, where [X] = molarity of X in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

5.9 What would be the equilibrium composition of a mixture prepared by mixing $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{D2O}$ with $80\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{H2O}$ at 298 K? Densities of pure $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{D2O}$ at 298 K are 997.05 and $1104.36\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, respectively. Assume ideal behavior of solution so that volumes are additive.

5.10 The self-dissociation constant of $\ce{D2O}$ is $1.1\times10^{-15}$ as compared to $1\times10^{-14}$ for $\ce{H2O}$. Here, the activities of the bulk liquids (not molarities) are used to determine dissociation constant. This shows that: (Mark X in the correct boxes)
a) O-H bond is stronger than O-D bond.
b) O-D bond is stronger than O-H bond.
c) $\ce{D2O}$ is a weaker acid than $\ce{H2O}$.
d) $\ce{D2O}$ is a stronger acid than $\ce{H2O}$.

Isotopic substitution, ideally, should not affect the chemical properties of the molecules since it does not affect the electronic configuration of the molecule. But in reality, the change of nucleus affects the strength of bonding. Changes in the rate of a reaction involving breaking of a bond involving H atoms versus the same bond involving D atom is known as the kinetic isotope effect.

5.11 Consider a reaction involving breaking of a C-H bond in a compound $\mathbf{Z}$ in the rate determining step. Which of the following would correctly represent the effect of deuterium substitution on concentration vs time profile of $\mathbf{Z}$ for the above reaction, keeping all other parameters constant? (Mark X in the correct box)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2017-5-fig2.png

problems.title: Lead Acid Batteries
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (20 marks). Lead Acid Batteries

Part A: Electrochemical processes in a lead acid cell

Conventional lead acid batteries used in cars and invertors are the most common rechargeable batteries in the market. A rechargeable lead acid cell consists of a positive electrode of $\ce{Pb(s)/PbO2(s)}$, and a negative electrode of $\ce{Pb(s)}$, both immersed in aqueous $\ce{H2SO4}$ electrolyte.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-1-fig1.png

Figure 1: Schematic of a conventional lead acid cell

Standard electrode potentials for some half-cell reactions at 298 K are given below.

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Half-Cell Reaction} & E^\circ\ (\mathrm{V}) \\ \hline \ce{PbO2(s) + SO4^{2-}(aq) + 4H+(aq) + 2e- -> PbSO4(s) + 2H2O(l)} & +1.69 \\ \ce{PbO2(s) + 4H+(aq) + 2e- -> Pb^{2+}(aq) + 2H2O(l)} & +1.46 \\ \ce{Pb^{2+}(aq) + 2e- -> Pb(s)} & -0.13 \\ \ce{PbSO4(s) + 2e- -> Pb(s) + SO4^{2-}(aq)} & -0.36 \end{array}$$

1.1 Write the half-cell reactions that take place at cathode and at anode in above cell during discharge at 298 K. Write the overall discharge reaction and calculate the $E^\circ$ of this cell.

Molar Enthalpies of formation ($H_f^\circ$) at 298 K of some species are given below.

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Species} & H_f^\circ\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{PbO2(s)} & -277.4 \\ \ce{H2O(l)} & -285.8 \\ \ce{Pb^{2+}(aq)} & 1.6 \\ \ce{SO4^{2-}(aq)} & -909.3 \\ \ce{PbSO4(s)} & -920.0 \end{array}$$

1.2 Calculate the standard enthalpy change ($\Delta H^\circ_{rxn}$) and standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta G^\circ_{rxn}$) for the overall discharge reaction of the cell in 1.1.

In a galvanic cell, the chemical energy released during the discharge reaction drives the electrical work. The Gibbs energy change of the discharge reaction represents the maximum electrical work $w_{\mathrm{max(el)}}$ that can be extracted from the cell during discharge.

$$w_{\mathrm{max(el)}} = -\Delta G^\circ_{rxn}$$

Maximum work is obtained when the cell is operated reversibly, i.e., at a very low current. Assume that the cell is designed to exchange heat with the surrounding to prevent overheating or overcooling.

1.3 For reversible operation of the cell at 298 K and all species in the cell in their standard states,

a) determine the amount of heat absorbed by the cell from the surrounding per mole of reaction as per the cell equation in 1.1.

b) what fraction of $w_{\mathrm{max(el)}}$ is obtained from the heat exchanged reversibly with the surroundings?

The concentration $c$ of a species in a solution is related to its activity $a$ as $a = \gamma \times c$, where $\gamma$ is the activity coefficient. For highly concentrated solutions, the reaction quotient $Q$ must be expressed in terms of activities of the species (i.e., $\gamma \neq 1$).

In commercial lead-acid batteries, highly concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ (aq.) is used. Conventionally, the liquid and solid components in a chemical reaction are assumed to be in their ‘standard states’ with activity as 1. However, due to the high concentration of sulfuric acid in the electrolyte, the activity of water also cannot be taken as 1.

1.4 For the discharge reaction of cell in 1.1, write the expression for the cell EMF in terms of activities of the species involved in the reaction. Consider $\ce{H2SO4}$ (aq.) to be completely dissociated and assume that only solids are in their standard states.

The lead-acid cell is considered to be discharged when the current that can be drawn from it decreases below a certain value. Discharge is also accompanied by a decrease in $\ce{H2SO4}$ concentration.

Activities of water and products of activities of relevant sulphuric acid species at 298 K in a lead acid cell are listed below at two concentrations of sulphuric acid.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & \ce{H2SO4}\ \text{Molality (m)} & a_{\ce{H2O}} & (a_{\ce{H+}})^2\cdot(a_{\ce{SO4^{2-}}}) \\ \hline 1 & 1.00 & 0.9618 & 0.0018 \\ 2 & 5.00 & 0.7032 & 0.8847 \end{array}$$

1.5 Assuming the discharged and charged states correspond to 1.00 molal and 5.00 molal $\ce{H2SO4}$, respectively, find the drop in the cell EMF values when it is discharged at 298 K.

Following are certain facts about the cell in Fig. 1.

(i) $\ce{PbSO4(s)}$ predominantly deposits on the electrodes and not in other parts of the cell.

(ii) $\ce{PbSO4(s)}$ deposits on both the electrodes.

(iii) Resistivity of $\ce{PbSO4(s)}$ deposits ($3 \times 10^{9}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}$) is much higher than that of $\ce{PbO2(s)}$ ($2 \times 10^{-4}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}$).

(iv) Resistivity of $\ce{PbO2(s)}$ ($2 \times 10^{-4}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}$) is close to that of $\ce{Pb(s)}$ ($0.2 \times 10^{-4}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}$).

1.6 Which of the above facts makes the cell rechargeable? (Write Statement number(s) i - iv, as applicable)

Electrolysis of water may become a competing process during charging of the cell in Fig. 1. The relevant half-cell reactions are given below.

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Half-Cell Reaction} & E^\circ\ (\mathrm{V}) \\ \hline \ce{O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e- -> 2H2O(l)} & +1.23 \\ \ce{2H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g)} & 0.00 \end{array}$$

1.7 For the operation of the cell in Fig.1 at 298 K, indicate whether the given statement is correct or incorrect. (Mark X in the appropriate box: Correct / Incorrect)

a. During charging of this cell, positive terminal of the DC power source is connected to the electrode that gets reduced, and negative terminal to the electrode that gets oxidised.

b. The EMF of the cell depends upon the amounts of the Pb species in the cell.

c. After a long-time of the lead-acid cell overcharging, the evolution of oxygen on one terminal and that of hydrogen on the other terminal may result in the formation of an explosive mixture of gases.

d. Upon completion of the charging process, oxygen starts to form on the negative electrodes.

e. The total energy stored in the cell is limited by the moles of $\ce{Pb(s)}$ in the negative electrode or the moles of $\ce{Pb^{4+}}$ in the positive electrode, whichever amount is less.

A different type of lead-based galvanic cell is given below. This cell has methane-sulphonic acid in which $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ has high solubility. The electrolyte consists of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ions dissolved in aqueous $\ce{CH3SO3H}$ in a cell having two inert electrodes. When external power supply is connected to this cell, $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ions are reduced at one electrode and oxidized at the other electrode, with the products depositing on the respective electrodes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-1-fig2.png

Figure 2: Simplified schematic of a lead acid cell based on methanesulphonic acid

1.8 Write the half-cell reactions that take place at cathode and at anode in the cell in Fig. 2 during discharge at 298 K. Write the overall discharge reaction and calculate the $E^\circ$ of this cell.

1.9 For the cell in Fig. 2, indicate whether the given statements are true or false (Mark X in the appropriate box: True / False).

a. Assuming that the volume of the electrolyte in this cell is kept constant, the pH of the electrolyte decreases during discharge of the cell.

b. The EMF of the cell increases with increasing $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ion concentration in the cell electrolyte.

c. The energy stored in the cell depends on the total amount of the Pb species in the cell.

Part B: Re-using spent batteries from cars and inverters

Recently a team of scientists showed that electrolyte for the lead acid cell in Figure 2 can be obtained by recycling the electrodes of a car battery. For this, the positive and negative plates of the spent battery (Fig.1) are thoroughly washed, separately dried and crushed into powders. Addition of excess aqueous methanesulfonic acid to these powders yields the electrolyte for the new lead acid cell (Fig.2).

1.10 Write balanced equations for the reactions involved in this conversion.

Some small-scale recyclers recover metallic $\ce{Pb(s)}$ from the electrodes of spent car batteries and throw away the $\ce{PbSO4(s)}$ slurry from the cell. It has been shown that a compound $\mathbf{X}$ useful for fabricating Pb-based thin film solar cells can be obtained from the slurry without high energy inputs. For this synthesis, the $\ce{PbSO4(s)}$ slurry is stirred overnight with a near-saturated solution of salt $\mathbf{A}$. This yields a white precipitate $\mathbf{B}$, which is collected by filtration.

1.11 Upon heating in a test tube, $\mathbf{A}$ decomposes into three colourless gases: an acidic gas, a basic gas and a neutral gas. Inserting a burning stick inside the test tube extinguished it, while a rod dipped in HCl brought close to the mouth of test tube generates white fumes. Identify $\mathbf{A}$ and hence $\mathbf{B}$.

Next, a weak monoprotic acid $\mathbf{C}$ is used to dissolve $\mathbf{B}$. 150 mg sample of $\mathbf{C}$ is completely neutralised by 25 mL of 0.1 M NaOH solution.

1.12 Calculate the molar mass of $\mathbf{C}$. Identify $\mathbf{C}$.

1.13 When excess of a halide salt that is used for treatment of hyper-thyroidism is added to the solution above, the yellow salt $\mathbf{X}$ precipitates out. Identify $\mathbf{X}$.

problems.title: When Rain meets the Soil
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (25 marks). When Rain meets the Soil

Part I: The fragrance of soil

When rain falls on soil after a dry period, a sweet earthy smell is produced known as the fragrance of first rain, which can be detected by camels even at a distance of 50 km. This scent has been captured in an increasingly famous scent “mitti ka itir” produced in Kannauj, India. This smell is due to the compounds geosmin ($\mathbf{A}$) and methyl-isoborneol ($\mathbf{B}$) produced by the actinobacteria present in soils.

On combustion, 0.455 g of ‘$\mathbf{A}$’ yields 1.318 g of $\ce{CO2}$.

2.1 Calculate the percentage of carbon in ‘$\mathbf{A}$’. Show the calculations involved.

‘$\mathbf{A}$’ undergoes dehydration easily under acidic condition to form an odourless hydrocarbon Argosmin ‘$\mathbf{C}$’. 0.455g of $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with sodium to liberate hydrogen gas which occupies $28.01\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ at STP.

2.2 Calculate the empirical formula of $\mathbf{A}$. Show the calculations involved.

$\mathbf{C}$ undergoes ozonolysis giving a single compound $\mathbf{D}$ which is further converted to $\mathbf{E}$ as follows.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-2-fig1.png

$\mathbf{E}$ can be synthesized by another route using cyclohexane-1,2-dione as shown below.

2.3 Draw the structures of the intermediate compounds and hence of $\mathbf{E}$ in the boxes provided.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-2-fig2.png

2.4 Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

2.5 $\mathbf{A}$ has three chiral centres. Draw all possible structural isomers of $\mathbf{A}$ consistent with the above information. (no stereo isomers are required)

The Cactaceae (cactus) family of plants grows in extremely hot and dry conditions and contain the compound dehydrogeosmin ‘$\mathbf{F}$’, which has ten times more odour than geosmin. It is believed to play a significant role in pollination in these plants.

$\mathbf{F}$ is converted to $\mathbf{A}$ by addition of one mole of $\ce{H2}$. The ozonolysis product of $\mathbf{F}$ gives a red precipitate with Fehling’s’ solution but does not give yellow precipitate with NaOH – $\ce{I2}$.

The dehydration product of $\mathbf{F}$, when subjected to ozonolysis gives the following products:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-2-fig3.png

$\mathbf{X}$ also does not give yellow precipitate with NaOH – $\ce{I2}$.

2.6 Draw the structure of $\mathbf{F}$ and hence $\mathbf{A}$.

The compound ‘$\mathbf{B}$’ can be synthesized by the following route.

2.7 Draw structures for $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ in the boxes provided.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-2-fig4.png

Part II: If the rain is acidic,…

As the water in clouds and rain drops equilibrates with atmosphere, it dissolves gases from the atmosphere. Usually, rain is slightly acidic because of dissolved $\ce{CO2}$ leading to a pH sometime as low as 5.6. The acidity of rain water in industrial areas is higher with pH as low as 3.5 to even 2 in some regions.

Natural water bodies often have carbonates of $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{K+}$, $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, and $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, dissolved from carbonate rocks, whose buffering action neutralizes acid in the rain. This buffering mechanism is important for sustaining aquatic life.

The carbonate buffer system is composed of various species and the equilibria between these species are governed by the following reactions.

$$\ce{CO2(g) <=> CO2(aq)}$$

$$\ce{CO2(aq) + H2O <=> H2CO3(aq)}$$

$$\ce{H2CO3(aq) + H2O <=> H3O+(aq) + HCO3^-(aq)} \qquad K_{a1} = 4.3 \times 10^{-7}$$

$$\ce{HCO3^-(aq) + H2O <=> H3O+(aq) + CO3^{2-}(aq)} \qquad K_{a2} = 4.8 \times 10^{-11}$$

The ability of a buffer to resist change in pH depends on the total concentration of the buffering species as well as their concentration ratio. Buffer capacity of a given solution is defined as the number of moles of a strong acid or a strong base that changes the pH of 1 L of the buffer by 1 unit.

A laboratory experiment was designed to simulate the buffering action of carbonate solutions, in which 300 mL of 0.004 M $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution was titrated against sulphuric acid and the following graph was obtained.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-2-fig5.png

2.8 Based on the graph, answer the following questions:

a. For what pH range(s), we cannot obtain buffers based on carbonate species?

b. What volume of 0.03 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ would change the pH of 1 L 0.004 M $\ce{Na2CO3}$ by 1 unit.

c. Buffer capacity of a $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution would

• i) Increase with the concentration of $\ce{Na2CO3(aq)}$
• ii) Remain unaffected by the concentration of $\ce{Na2CO3(aq)}$
• iii) Decrease with the concentration of $\ce{Na2CO3(aq)}$

Next, let us do some simple calculations to understand the buffering action of a $\ce{CaCO3}$ solution. A saturated solution of $\ce{CaCO3}$ (solubility = $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ M) was prepared in distilled water. Assume that the distilled water was free of any dissolved gases and any other cations.

2.9 Calculate the pH of the saturated $\ce{CaCO3}$ solution. (Hint: amount of $\ce{H2CO3(aq)}$ formed under these conditions would be negligible.)

2.10 Determine what volume of 0.03 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ would be required to lower the pH of 300 mL of saturated $\ce{CaCO3}$ solution by 1unit. Assume that the volume change of the $\ce{CaCO3}$ solution due to acid addition is small.

2.11 If the saturated solution of $\ce{CaCO3}$ is in contact with excess solid $\ce{CaCO3}$, the buffer capacity of this system would be (Mark X in the appropriate box)

• a. same as that of the saturated solution.
• b. more than that of the saturated solution.
• c. lower than that of the saturated solution.

2.12 Comparing the saturated solutions of $\ce{MgCO3}$ ($K_{sp} = 6.8 \times 10^{-6}$) and $\ce{CaCO3}$ ($K_{sp} = 2.8 \times 10^{-9}$), the correct statements is (Mark X in the appropriate box)

• a. Buffer capacities of both the solutions are equal
• b. Buffer capacity of $\ce{MgCO3}$ solution will be more than that of $\ce{CaCO3}$
• c. Buffer capacity of $\ce{CaCO3}$ solution will be more than that of $\ce{MgCO3}$

2.13 Among $\ce{Na2CO3}$, $\ce{MgCO3}$, and $\ce{CaCO3}$, identify the salts that fit the following descriptions and write the formula in the boxes provided.

(i) For equal volumes of saturated solutions of the three salts taken separately, solution of this salt will provide the best buffering action against acid.

(ii) After heavy rains, this salt is found only in dissolved forms in water bodies, no deposits are found in soils.

(iii) In regions receiving very high rainfall annually, deposits of this salt remain for centuries, and provide a major source of carbonate buffering against acidic rain for the longest period of time.

Acidic rain in regions lacking sufficient buffering substances lead to acidification of the water bodies, which is often detected by the loss of the sweet smell of geosmin from the region.

problems.title: Hydrogen Bonding and Water of Crystallization
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (21 marks). Hydrogen Bonding and Water of Crystallization

Part 1

Water is the most abundant molecule on the earth’s surface. Water makes a major fraction of the mass of the biological as well as many non-biological entities. Water is liquid at room temperature because of extensive intermolecular hydrogen-bonding. A molecule containing H covalently bonded to an electronegative atom is known as a hydrogen bond donor, whereas a molecule with electron-rich atom which makes H-bond with an H atom is known as a hydrogen bond acceptor.

3.1 Identify the molecules in the figure below which would act as H-bond donors, H-bond acceptors or both (write the corresponding number/s in the box/es)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig1.png

• (a) Only hydrogen bond acceptors
• (b) Only hydrogen bond donors
• (c) Both, as hydrogen bond donors and acceptors

Hydrogen bond is represented by a dotted line (----) while a covalent bond is represented by a solid line. For some compounds, intermolecular H-bonding leads to formation of porous frameworks with specific pore sizes. Such frameworks can be used to selectively trap small molecules like $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{SO2}$, etc. in an atmosphere.

Xenon is a modern anaesthetic that has been successfully used in surgeries, which shows its ability to interact with other molecules. One challenge with this use is high cost of production, and ease of storage and transport. Interestingly, Xe can be reversibly trapped in porous three-dimensional frameworks of molecules such as water, quinol, etc, held together by H-bonds.

Slow evaporation of an aqueous solution of p-quinol saturated with Xe yields crystal of p-quinol framework. X-ray crystallography of these crystals indicates six p-quinols organized around one Xe atom. The phenyl rings in p-quinols are in cyclic arrangement positioned alternately above and below a plane. This arrangement generates hexagonal cavities in the structure.

The unit cell for Xe-encapsulated p-quinol crystal is shown below. Two molecules of p-quinol are centered at two opposite face centers, 8 molecules are centered at the edge centers, while the rest are inside the cell body.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig2.png

A view of the above unit cell as seen along the c-axis is given in the box below, with C, O, and Xe atoms labelled (H atoms are not labelled in the structure).

3.2 Show the hydrogen bonds that define the hexagonal cavities in the structure given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig3.png

3.3 By referring to the unit cell diagrams given above, calculate the number of p-quinol molecules and the number of Xe atoms present per unit cell. Show the steps involved in arriving at the answer.

The cell parameters for the above unit cell are: $a = 16.58$ Å, $b = 16.58$ Å, $c = 5.42$ Å, $\alpha = \beta = 90^\circ$, $\gamma = 120^\circ$.

3.4 Determine the density of this crystal (in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$), assuming all the hexagonal cavities in the crystal are occupied by Xe atoms.

3.5 If all the hexagonal cavities in the crystal are occupied by Xe atoms, calculate the volume that Xe trapped in $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of p-quinol framework would occupy when released at 298 K and 1 atm.

Part B: Water of crystallization

Water of crystallization is the amount of water necessary for certain salts to crystallize from their solutions. Studies have shown that water of crystallization forms bonds with the ions of the salt and stabilizes the crystal structure. This water also affects the shapes and colour of their crystals.

Blue-green crystals of $\ce{CuCl2.2H2O}$ on heating lose water giving brown coloured anhydrous salt. The unit cell of anhydrous $\ce{CuCl2}$ is shown below where each copper is in square planar coordination and all Cu-Cl distances are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig4.png

3.6 This ionic arrangement is stabilized because (Mark X in the correct box(es)):

• (i) Every $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ is stabilized by two $\ce{Cl-}$ present perpendicular to the $\ce{CuCl4}$ plane.
• (ii) Every $\ce{Cl-}$ is stabilized by two $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ present perpendicular to the $\ce{CuCl4}$ plane.
• (iii) This structure has FCC arrangement of the $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions.
• (iv) Layers of $\ce{Cl-}$ ions are next to each other and are sandwiched between the layers of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions.

When $\ce{CuCl2}$ is exposed to moisture, water enters the space between the ions forming $\ce{CuCl2.2H2O}$. The water molecules induce many changes such as shift of Cu-Cl units with respect to each other and changes in Cu-Cl distances. $\ce{CuCl2.2H2O}$ crystallizes in an end-centered orthorhombic lattice stabilized by hydrogen bonds. The $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions occupy all the vertices and centres of two opposite faces.

The following table shows four possible framework positions of $\ce{Cl-}$ ions with respect to $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions. Out of the four frameworks given, three are not observed because of one or more of the following reasons:

I. The structure would have high inter-ionic repulsions, which cannot be effectively minimized by the two molecules of water per $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ion.

II. The cell shown is not a unit cell because it cannot be repeated to generate a lattice.

III. The ratio of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$:$\ce{Cl-}$ ions is not 1:2 per unit cell.

3.7 Identify the impossible frameworks by writing the correct reasoning statement (give number I, II or III) against the structure. In the correct framework, show water molecules with appropriate bonds with the ions present.

[Table with two columns: “Framework” and “Reason/s for impossible framework wherever applicable”; the four frameworks are shown below in the printed order, the second column is left empty for the answers.]

[Framework 1]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig5.png

[Framework 2]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig6.png

[Framework 3]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig7.png

[Framework 4]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-3-fig8.png

Materials which can store and release thermal energy by absorbing water molecules are promising heat storage systems. Salts like $\ce{CuCl2.2H2O}$ can be dehydrated by keeping in the sunlight, which is an endothermic process. The anhydrous salts then can be used to heat a room by exposure to water vapours. These salt-based devices can be dehydrated and hydrated again and again.

In search of a thermal energy storage material, a student checked the amount of energy released by anhydrous $\ce{CuCl2}$ on exposure to water. The student added 2.5 g anhydrous $\ce{CuCl2}$ to 50 mL water (initially at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) in a covered polystyrene cup and noted $3.2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ rise in temperature.

3.8 Assuming that the polystyrene cup is a closed and thermally insulated system and the specific heat of water (with dissolved salts) is $4.18\,\mathrm{J\,^\circ C^{-1}\,g^{-1}}$, calculate the amount of heat released (enthalpy of hydration) by anhydrous $\ce{CuCl2}$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Lignin
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (19 marks). Lignin

Lignin is a biopolymer that constitutes 15 - 40% of the dry weight of plants. Its major function is to provide structural support to the plant. Lignin has the potential of yielding several industrially important chemicals, a concept known as Bio refinery (similar to petroleum refinery). A major challenge in this conversion is the depolymerization of lignin. A representative structure of lignin is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-4-fig1.png

4.1 In the above structure of lignin, identify the functional groups present. (Mark X against the correct option/s)

• a) Diaryl ether
• b) Aryl alkyl ether
• c) Ester
• d) 1º Amino
• e) Lactone
• f) 2º Alcohol

Direct chemical depolymerization of lignin is a difficult process. Oxidized forms of lignin can be depolymerized, but it is expensive and involves hazardous reagents. In 2014, a group led by an American scientist Shannon S. Stahl showed that formic acid in the presence of sodium formate can be used efficiently to depolymerize the oxidized forms of lignin. To understand the mechanism of this process, model compounds $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ that represent structural units of lignin and oxidized lignin, respectively, were prepared. Following scheme illustrates the synthesis of $\mathbf{D}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-4-fig2.png

4.2 Identify structures of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

$\mathbf{D}$ on oxidation using $\ce{CrO3/H2SO4}$ gave an unexpected product $\mathbf{E}$ and two minor products. $\mathbf{E}$ gives no reaction with Tollen’s reagent or with saturated $\ce{NaHCO3}$.

4.3 Identify structure of $\mathbf{E}$.

$$\mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\ce{CrO3/H2SO4}} \mathbf{E}\ (\ce{C18H20O6})$$

Both model compounds $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ were treated with excess formic acid in the presence of aqueous sodium formate at room temperature to give products $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, respectively.

4.4 Identify structures of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

$$\mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}]{\text{excess } \ce{HCOOH/HCOONa}} \mathbf{F}$$

$$\mathbf{E} \xrightarrow[25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}]{\text{excess } \ce{HCOOH/HCOONa}} \mathbf{G}\ (\ce{C19H20O7})$$

On heating with excess formic acid in aqueous sodium formate at $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ gave only $\mathbf{F}$, whereas, $\mathbf{E}$ gave a mixture of $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$, and $\mathbf{J}$. For this reaction of $\mathbf{E}$ at $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, variation in the amounts of $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{J}$ over time is presented in Plot 1.

When $\mathbf{G}$ was heated with formic acid in aqueous sodium formate to $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ were obtained. For this reaction, variation in the amounts of $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ with time are given in Plot 2. The rates of formation of $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ were same.

4.5 Identify the curves corresponding to $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ in Plots 1, and for $\mathbf{J}$ in Plot 2. (Write the appropriate letter in the corresponding boxes in the plots)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-4-fig3.png

4.6 From the curve for $\mathbf{H}$ in plot 2, we can infer that (Mark X in the correct box/es)

C-H bond and its Deuterium analogue, C-D bond, differ in their bond energies. This difference in bond energies also affects the rate of reactions where these bonds are involved. problems.title: Keto-Enol Tautomerism: Kinetics and Thermodynamics
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (22 marks). Keto-Enol Tautomerism: Kinetics and Thermodynamics

Two compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural arrangement of atoms in molecules are known as structural isomers, e.g., $\ce{C2H6O}$ represents both ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether. One form of structural isomerism is tautomerism, in which the same molecule dynamically interconverts between two or more structural forms. Carbonyl compounds exhibit keto-enol tautomerism, represented as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-5-fig1.png

5.1 For the following compound, write the possible tautomers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-5-fig2.png

Many carbonyl compounds with acidic alpha hydrogen are important for industrial synthesis of many chemicals. Ethyl acetoacetate (EAA), i.e., ethyl-3-oxo butanoate is one such widely used compound. In solution, EAA is an equilibrium mixture of the keto and an enol form.

5.2 Draw the structures of possible enol forms for EAA and identify the most stable enol form.

The most stable enol form is observed experimentally. To study the kinetics of the following reaction, a detailed experiment was conducted.

$$\text{EAA(Keto)} \underset{k_\mathrm{B}}{\overset{k_\mathrm{F}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{EAA(Enol)} \qquad (1)$$

Four flasks ($\mathbf{A}$ - $\mathbf{D}$) were taken, each containing 25 mL solution $\mathbf{S}$ of EAA ($15\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$) in anhydrous methanol. The flasks were maintained at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ throughout this study. Excess of freshly prepared bromine solution in methanol (25 mL) at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ was added rapidly to each flask at $t = 0$ s. The enol form reacts extremely rapidly with bromine while the keto form does not. This reaction results in an acidic solution. Bromination of enol is a very fast reaction compared to the enolization of EAA. The mono-brominated ester formed is stable and doesn’t react further under these reaction conditions.

5.3 Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction that would take place on addition of bromine to solution $\mathbf{S}$.

Excess of 2,4,4-trimethyl-1-pentene was added rapidly to flasks $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ at $t$ = 10, 40, 75, and 100 s, respectively.

5.4 The 2,4,4-trimethyl-1-pentene added will (Mark X in the appropriate box(es))

• (i) increase the rate of keto to enol conversion.
• (ii) consume unreacted bromine.
• (iii) react with monobrominated ester and hence ensure complete bromination of EAA.
• (iv) stop the enolization reaction.

After addition of 2,4,4-trimethyl-1-pentene, about 10 mL of 10% aqueous KI solution was added to each of the flasks $\mathbf{A}$ - $\mathbf{D}$ and allowed to stand for 30 minutes. The reaction mixture was still acidic. During this time, brominated ester is converted back to EAA. Then, the liberated iodine is titrated with 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate solution using starch indicator. Assume that there is no reaction between iodine and any form of EAA.

5.5 Write the balanced equation of the reaction for the liberation of iodine.

5.6 Write the balanced equation for reaction of iodine with sodium thiosulphate.

The experiment can be summarized as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-5-fig3.png

Following volumes of sodium thiosulphate solution were consumed in titration with the solutions in the flasks $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Flask} & \text{Volume of } \ce{Na2S2O3} \text{ solution used (mL)} \\ \hline \mathbf{A} & 3.78 \\ \mathbf{B} & 4.02 \\ \mathbf{C} & 4.30 \end{array}$$

5.7 From this data, find $n_\mathrm{keto}$, the number of moles of keto form of EAA at the time of addition of 2,4,4-trimethyl-1-pentene, for the flasks $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. Show detailed calculations for flask $\mathbf{A}$. You may assume volumes to be additive during mixing of solutions in this experiment.

The following graph indicates the plot of $-\ln(n_\mathrm{keto})$ versus time ($t$). Point corresponding to flask $\mathbf{D}$ is indicated on the graph.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2018-5-fig4.png

5.8 Plot the values corresponding to flasks $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in the graph above. Using the graph, find the following for conversion of EAA (keto) to EAA (enol) in reaction (1).

a. The order of the reaction.

b. Rate constant $k_\mathrm{F}$ for the reaction.

c. Equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{eq}$ for the reaction. Report the answer upto 5 significant figures.

When the above experiment was carried out at $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the values of $K_\mathrm{F}$ and $K_\mathrm{eq}$ were found to be $5.25 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and 0.06272, respectively.

5.9 Using the above information, find the values of $\Delta H^\circ$ (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and $\Delta S^\circ$ (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$) for the enolization reaction (1). Assume $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ to be independent of temperature. Show necessary calculations.

Reaction kinetics is very important for the industrial use of a reaction, as the reaction rates affect the time in which a certain amount of product can be synthesised. This time of production in turn affects the cost of the final product.

An industrialist has 8.5 kg of EAA and hopes to produce compound $\mathbf{Y}$ (Molar mass = 174 g), which is obtained in equimolar amount from the Enol form of EAA.

$$\text{EAA (Keto)} \underset{k_\mathrm{B}}{\overset{k_\mathrm{F}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{EAA(Enol)} \xrightarrow{k'} \mathbf{Y}$$

5.10 For what value of $k'$, the industrialist would obtain a certain amount of $\mathbf{Y}$ in minimum amount of time? (Mark X in the appropriate box(es))

• (i) $k' \approx 0$
• (ii) $k' \to$ infinity

5.11 The industrialist did not know the value of $k'$, but wanted to know the minimum time that would be required to produce 10 kg of $\mathbf{Y}$ using the available EAA in methanol as solvent at $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Estimate this time assuming that (i) the kinetics of the enolization reaction of EAA in this large scale reaction is same as determined in the laboratory experiment described above and (ii) other effects such as changes in temperature and solution volume during the progress of reaction are negligible.

problems.title: Common and Uncommon Amino Acids
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (23 marks). Common and Uncommon Amino Acids

Proteins are the most diverse class of biologically important compounds, derived from structurally varied α-amino acids. However, α-amino acids are not just found as the building blocks of proteins, but serve a variety of other functions too. This capacity of amino acids is derived due to their unique structure. Here, we will first look at the common properties of amino acids and then two special amino acids.

Part I

α-Amino acids have at least two $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values, one of the $\ce{-COOH}$ group and the other of the conjugate acid of the amino group. The two $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values of the amino acid proline are $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 1.95$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2} = 10.64$.

1.1 Write the predominant equilibria in aqueous solutions of proline at pH = 1.95 and 10.64.

α-Amino acids are usually characterized by their isoelectric pH (written as pI), which is the pH at which the degree of protonation at one functional group in the amino acid equals the degree of deprotonation at another functional group in the amino acid. At this pH, the amino acid shows minimum/zero electrical conductivity in aqueous solution and predominantly exists in electrically-neutral zwitter ionic form.

1.2 Based on the above definition of pI, derive a relation between pI, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1}$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2}$ for proline.

1.3 Consider the following statements for the amino acid and mark X in the correct box/es.

a. The $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{-COOH}$ group in an α-amino acid is lower than the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of acetic acid. (True / False)

b. The $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{-NH3+}$ group in an α-amino acid is lower than the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{-NH3+}$ group derived from a primary amine. (True / False)

1.4 When the side chain of the α-amino acid bears an additional acidic or basic functional group, they are classified as acidic or basic amino acids, respectively. The amino acid arginine has three $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$'s in the pH range 0 – 14.

a. For arginine, the most likely $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values are (Mark X in the correct box)

• i. 1.2, 2.0, 9.0
• ii. 3.1, 5.0, 12.3
• iii. 3.0, 6.7, 12.1
• iv. 2.2, 9.0, 12.5

b. In the following structure of arginine, circle the groups involved in proton exchange and assign appropriate $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values based on your answer in 1.4a.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/in-2019-1-fig1.png

c. Write the structure for the zwitter ionic form of arginine amino acid and also for the species that is formed by the addition of one $\ce{H+}$ to this zwitter ion. [Answer box headed: Zwitter Ion; Zwitter ion + $\ce{H+}$.]

d. Calculate the pI value of arginine. Show the steps involved in calculations.

Chromatography is a technique used to separate species in a mobile phase (liquid or gaseous) on the basis of their distribution between stationery and mobile phases. The ion exchange chromatographic technique exploits the interaction between charged entities in the mobile phase and the charged groups present in the solid stationary phase—usually an ion exchange resin.

The following figure indicates one type of ion exchange resin ($\mathbf{X}$) that contains $\ce{SO3- Na+}$ groups as shown. The counter ion $\ce{Na+}$ can be exchanged with the positive ions present in the mobile phase and hence, the resin is called cation-exchange resin.
